en: The Kṛtyakalpataru composed by Śrī Lakṣmīdhara:
The Section on Purification (Śuddhikāṇḍa)
Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa. [Oṃ, salutations to the Blessed One Vāsudeva.
Auspicious Invocation.
[1] By means of his gold— which is exceedingly pure due to its color and its acquisition through proper means— the twice-born have attained purification from both poverty and evil deeds.
In this tenth book, Lakṣmīdhara— the rising mountain for the moon of Dharma,
the best among the pure, and a treasury of the waters of right conduct— composes this [treatise on] purification.
Now, the formal proposition:
impurity on death, as well as impurity on birth, and all the restrictive rules pertaining to those two; furthermore, there is impurity in the case of the mixture of castes.
[2] Now, impurity (āśauca) arising from a fatal illness, likewise impurity when one has gone abroad,
impurity concerning infants and others, impurity concerning women, and thereafter impurity due to miscarriage.

There is especially no impurity upon the death of a Mṛyu, nor likewise when one who is not a sapinda has died; furthermore, there is no impurity for those who carry out the corpse and so forth, and for those who are otherwise free from impurity.
The definition of sapinda-relationship, the removal of the deceased, the funeral rites for the dead,
the offering of water to the deceased, and the determination of those entitled to the water-offering.
Likewise, the removal of grief, entering one's own home, the collection of bones, and the purification through bathing the body; these are the stages.
Likewise, in this context, [one should explain] the purification of substances, as well as purification when [something] is extremely defiled,
the purification of the ground, the purification of water, and the removal of impurity.
In the tenth chapter on purification, Lakṣmīdhara,
whose intellect is purified by the knowledge of reality, sequentially [describes] twenty-eight observances (*parvan*).
[3] 1 Now, regarding impurity due to death.
Regarding purification after death,
Manu [5.58] says:
"I shall now declare the purification for the deceased, as well as the purification of objects."
Of all four castes as well, in due order and according to their respective status.
The mention of "ghosts" (*preta*) is also an elliptical indication for those who have been born [into the state of existence].

Hārīta says: "Purification (*śauca*) is indeed of two kinds: external and internal. Among these, the external is threefold: purification of the family (*kula*), purification of food (*anna*), and purification of the body (*śarīra*). In cases of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) and death-impurity (*mṛtaka*), there is impurity for the family on both sides for ten nights."
"From both" means from both [occasions], namely birth and death. Devala says:
"Impurity invariably follows upon birth and death."
One may go anywhere to visit one's sapindas and maternal kinsmen.
[4] Impurity is prescribed for those born of the same womb, for kinsmen, for the twice-born, and for co-residents;
likewise, there shall be impurity caused by death or birth for husbands and teachers.
One who goes [to serve] for a specific purpose does not incur that impurity of servitude; thus, he does not become subject to it.

In the phrase "among those born of the same womb, kinsmen, and twice-born" (*yonijñātidvijeṣu*), the word *yoni* refers to paternal relatives. "Kinsmen" (*jñātayaḥ*) refers to those who are *sakulyas*, distinct from the *sapiṇḍas*. The term "co-residents" (*sahavāsiṣu*) is, by implication, an adjective qualifying the twice-born, because others—such as paternal relatives and so forth—are subject to impurity even if they do not reside together.
(Manu 5.59)
Impurity on account of a death is prescribed for ten days among the sapindas;
it may last for three days or even one day until the collection of the bones.
Śaṅkha says: "O best of the twice-born, upon birth or death,
a Sapiṇḍa who is endowed with the sacred fires and the Vedas attains purity after three days."
Bṛhaspati [Āśauca 23.21]:
A Brāhmaṇa who maintains the Veda and the sacred fires becomes pure after three nights;
one who lacks the sacred fires becomes pure after five days; and one who merely bears the name of a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure after ten days.
[5] Where Vedic recitation is performed, where oblations are offered at both times of day,
and where the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice is constantly maintained, there impurity is not found.
Dakṣa says:
Immediate purification, as well as one day, three days,
four days, six, ten, twelve days, a fortnight, and likewise a month.
Likewise, there is another [impurity] ending at death; however, regarding the ten categories of birth-impurity (sūtaka), I shall explain them in their proper order and in their entirety.

If one understands the Veda together with its limbs, along with the ritual manuals and secret doctrines, both in letter and in meaning, and is engaged in the performance of rites, there is no impurity due to birth or death.

Since the word *aṅga* (limb/part) itself already implies a ritual manual (*kalpa*), the explicit mention of *kalpa* again is for the purpose of including even the manuals of other Vedic branches (*paraśākhā*) that are useful for one's own performance. "Secret" (*rahasya*) refers to the revelation of the Self by way of the Upaniṣads. "One who performs the rites" (*kriyāvān*) means one who maintains the Śrauta fires. "No impurity from birth" (*na sūtakaṃ*) means immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*).
Dakṣa says:
"A Brahmin who is endowed with the sacred fires and the Vedas is purified in a single day."
In the case of the inferior [offense], it is even more inferior: three days and likewise four days.

“Hīnaḥ” (inferior) refers to one who maintains the Smārta fires and studies only a portion of the Veda. “Hīnataraḥ” (more inferior) refers to one who is devoid of both Śrauta and Smārta fires but studies the complete Veda.
[6] Parāśara [3.18; 5.19]: Where the sacred fires are offered, or where the Veda is recited...
The Vaiśvadeva offering must indeed be performed constantly; there is no impurity during birth or death.

“*Nāśaucam*” (no impurity) refers to the intent of immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*). In the case of a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) residing at home where the sacrificial fire is maintained, there is neither impurity from death nor from birth for those who have ceased all social contact [with the outside world].
A Brahmin who is endowed with the sacred fires and the Vedas becomes pure in one day;
one who possesses only the Vedas in three days; but one devoid of qualities [becomes pure] in ten days.
A Brahmin becomes impure through contact during births and deaths;
for those who have withdrawn from such contacts, there is neither impurity from death nor impurity from birth.

By the plural number in the word “fires,” the triad of fires is understood. In the phrase “or the Veda,” the word “or” (vā) signifies conjunction. Here, “contact” refers to sitting, sleeping, eating, and so forth, together with another sapinda who is pure. “One who possesses only the Veda” here means one who maintains the Smārta fire and studies the Veda, but not one who is devoid of fire altogether, because the rule for purification is prescribed after five days; as Bṛhaspati says, following the word “he shall be purified”:
“One devoid of the [Śrauta] fire is purified in five days, but a nominal Brāhmaṇa (brāhmaṇabruva) in ten days. Thus says Jābāli.

Those endowed with one, two, or three qualities [of purity] are declared to be purified immediately through the performance of all [required] rites, according to the sequence of four, three, and two days respectively.
All [others], however, are declared to be purified immediately by the performance of every [necessary] rite.

“One who possesses one quality” (*ekaguṇaḥ*) is one who studies only the Veda. “One who possesses two qualities” (*dviguṇaḥ*) is one who maintains the Smārta fires in addition to the Veda. “One who possesses three qualities” (*triguṇaḥ*) is one who maintains the Śrauta fires in addition to the Smārta and Vedic fires. “All” refers to Brāhmaṇas. “Possession of all qualities” (*sarvayoga*) refers to the possession of the qualities mentioned in the statement, “he understands [the Veda] both by its words and its meaning. And here, the intended meaning of these statements is as follows: the impurity that has been declared here regarding a person who fully understands the words and meaning of the Veda along with its auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*) and performs rites such as the *agnihotra*, should be understood to apply only when he is not in contact with an impure son or other such persons.
A Brahmin becomes defiled by contact, both at birth and at death;
for those who have desisted from such contact, there is neither the state of a ghost nor the impurity of childbirth.

[8] Because it is stated thus by Parāśara: "Even for such a person, when there is contact with the impurity (*aśauca*) of a son or other relative, impurity occurs just as it does for those who are themselves impure. And in this way, it is logical that even for those who maintain the Veda and the *Agnihotra*, there is the practice of purification after ten days for those with whom they have come into contact. Furthermore, for a person of this kind who studies only the Veda but has not investigated its meaning—who maintains the *Agnihotra* (the fire-ritual) or possesses the Vedic study and the *Smārta* fire—impurity lasts for one day or three days solely due to contact with such a person. And it is on account of such a scope for impurity that the absence of impurity regarding activities such as maintaining the *Agnihotra*, as stated by Viṣṇu, Gautama, and others in passages such as "For those who maintain the *Agnihotra*, the *Agnihotra* [is not interrupted]," becomes logically consistent. It is not appropriate to restrict a scripture that applies specifically to a particular case to the scope of those who live from day to day (*āśvastanika*) and so forth, because there is no evidence for such a restriction in this form. Nor does the injunction regarding the livelihood of living from day to day imply a restriction of impurity; for the injunction regarding the livelihood of living from day to day is logically applicable to persons who avoid contact with those who are pure and qualified by qualities such as knowledge of the meaning of the Veda. Or, if the restriction of impurity is intended to apply to persons who possess qualities such as knowledge of the Veda's meaning and are free from contact with the impure, [then the rule stands].
"He understands the Veda together with its auxiliary sciences (aṅgas) both by way of the text and the meaning"; likewise, "where the fires are offered," and similarly,
"among those who have withdrawn from social contacts, there is neither impurity on account of death nor impurity on account of birth."

Statements such as these are indeed the authority (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, regarding the fact that Dakṣa and Parāśara have prescribed one-day impurity (*ekāhāśauca*) for those endowed with the *Śrauta* and *Vaidika* fires, while Śaṅkha and Bṛhaspati have prescribed three-day impurity (*tryahāśauca*), a systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) according to the respective order is appropriate, because there is no overlap between the scope of the statements on one-day and three-day impurity. This is established by taking them as referring respectively to those possessing *Śrauta* and *Smārta* fires. For the statement concerning one-day impurity applies to a person possessing *Śrauta* fires, since such a person is more venerable than one possessing only *Smārta* fires. Jābāli says:
"Thus, those endowed with two, three, or four qualities [of fire] are [subject to] four, three, or one [day of impurity] respectively."
All [of these], by every means, are proclaimed to be immediately purified.

Baudhāyana [1.11.1], speaking with reference to birth and death, states: "Impurity lasts for ten days among *sapiṇḍas*," excluding the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), those initiated for sacrifice (*dīkṣita*), and religious students (*brahmacārin*). Because they are *sapiṇḍas*, the impurity that would otherwise apply to the officiating priests and others upon the birth or death of a *sapiṇḍa* is here prohibited. Uśanas says:
"In that regard, for birth and death occurring at a different time or in a different place, the period is ten nights."
“Of time and another place” means those not separated by space or time.
[10] Manu [5.64]: “In one day and one night, and in three sets of three nights...”
Those who touch a corpse become pure after three days, as do those who offer water for them.

“Three times three nights” means nine days and nights. Likewise, one day and one night constitute a single *ahorātra*. Thus, ten days are completed. “Those who touch a corpse” are those who carry out the dead. “Givers of water” are the *samānodaka* (distant sapindas). This is the essential meaning here: if those who are *sapiṇḍas* or *samānodakas* by virtue of being endowed with qualities such as conduct and Vedic study should, out of affection or other reasons, become touchers of a corpse, then they shall observe impurity for ten days or three days respectively. Bṛhaspati [Āśauca 29]:
[11] Within ten days, those who are *sapiṇḍas* become pure after a death or birth;
those who are *sakulyas*, being members of the same lineage (*gotra*), become pure by bathing after three nights.

“Sakulyas” are those related by water (samānodakas). “Gotrajas” are sapindas other than the sakulyas. Gautama [14.22–27]: Upon touching a corpse, there is impurity for ten nights if it was intentional. This has been stated regarding Vaishyas and Shudras. Or, in the case of women during their menses, or in the case of the two preceding castes (Brahmins and Kshatriyas), there is a three-day period of impurity.

“Touching” (*upasparśanam*) here means carrying out [the corpse]. “If intentionally” (*abhisaṃdhāya cet*) means that if one touches a corpse having accepted it as visible [to the senses], then this impurity applies; but not in the case of one acting for the sake of *dharma*, *artha*, or *kāma*. And for a Brāhmaṇa, this applies only upon touching another Brāhmaṇa, because the Vaiśya and Śūdra are mentioned separately. Upon touching a Kṣatriya, however, only his own [specific] impurity occurs. This is established by the connection with the attainment of purity through the mention of the first and the last, which implies the middle. “It has been stated for the Vaiśya and Śūdra”: but for the Vaiśya and Śūdra separately, when touching a deceased person of their own caste, that which was previously stated—namely twelve nights and so forth—is exactly what applies. “Menstrual” (*ārtavīḥ*): for the Vaiśya and Śūdra, the impurity lasts for nights equal in number to the menstrual period, or six or five nights. “For the two former”: for the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya mentioned previously, the impurity is either that of the menstrual period or the previously mentioned three days. These options are established in consideration of the excellence or deficiency of their conduct (*vṛtta*).
Now, Parāśara [3.9, 3.6]: A Brāhmaṇa becomes pure after three days in the case of birth or death involving a deceased person;
a Kṣatriya becomes pure after twelve days in the case of birth or death involving a deceased person.
[12] A Vaiśya becomes pure in fifteen days, and one who has fallen away from his birth-rites and duties and has abandoned the twilight devotions (saṃdhyopāsana) becomes pure in a month.
But a Brāhmaṇa who merely bears the name [of his caste] becomes pure after ten days.
Devala says:
"The purification for a Śūdra is by thirty days; for a Vaiśya, by twenty days."
For a king, [the impurity lasts] fifteen days; for a Brahmin, ten days.
Others, however, know that in all cases of impurity, whether at death or at birth, the period lasts ten nights,
seeing the exhaustion of the ritual action.

Gautama [14.1–5]: Impurity on account of a corpse lasts ten nights for the *sapiṇḍas* of those who are officiating priests, consecrated for a sacrifice, or celibate students. For a Kṣatriya it lasts eleven nights; for a Vaiśya, twelve nights; some say half a month; and for a Śūdra, one month. Śātātapa says:

Impurity due to death (*śāva-āśauca*) for a Brāhmaṇa is purified after ten nights; for a Kṣatriya, after twelve nights; for a Vaiśya, after half a month. For a Śūdra, because he is exempt from the necessity of reciting mantras, there is neither entitlement nor prohibition [regarding this period]. "Abiding in that" means one becomes impure for that same duration as the person [whose death caused it]; "that" refers to the caste of the Brāhmaṇa and so forth, and "abiding in that" means one remains impure for such a length of time. [13] Yājñavalkya.
For a Kṣatriya, it is twelve days; for a Vaiśya, fifteen;
for a Śūdra, thirty days; but for one who lives righteously, it is half of that.

"For those who live according to the law" (*nyāyavartinaḥ*)—meaning for one devoted to the *pākayajña* sacrifices and the service of the twice-born—"that which is appropriate for them" (*tadarham*) shall apply.
Manu [5.140]: "For Śūdras who live according to the law, shaving of the head should be performed monthly."
Their rules for purification are like those of a Vaiśya, and their food consists of the remnants of a twice-born man's meal.
Jābāli says:
For a king, the period of impurity lasts twelve or twenty days after slaughter;
for a Śūdra, it is one month; for the remaining castes, the rule is that impurity lasts as long as [the body remains].
Yama says: In the case of death or birth impurity, a Brāhmaṇa becomes pure after ten nights;
a Vaiśya after twenty nights; and a Kṣatriya (lord of the earth) after fifteen days.
Likewise, a Śūdra is always purified by a full month;
this purification has been observed by me in brief for the four castes.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "Women of the [upper] castes should observe purity and impurity just as Śūdras do. Paiṭhīnasi:

For a Brāhmaṇa, there is a period of impurity lasting ten days on account of birth or death; for a Kṣatriya, sixteen days; for a Vaiśya, twenty nights; and for a Śūdra, one month. Beyond this, we shall explain the conduct of the social classes in their proper order, as well as the impurity caused by death (śāva-āśauca) as it has been observed by the wise.
On the fourth day, the touching [of the body] must indeed be performed for the Brāhmaṇa;
however, on the eleventh day here, purification occurs, as do the rites of giving and Vedic study.
On the fifth day, however, the touch of a Kṣatriya is to be known;
on the seventh day, the touch of a Vaiśya is to be understood by the wise.
In this case, the purification for a Kṣatriya shall always be by twelve days;
however, the purification regarding food for a Vaiśya is prescribed as half a month.
On the tenth day, the wise should perform the touching of a Śūdra;
however, purification occurs after one full month in the case of both birth-impurity (sūtaka) and death-impurity (mṛtaka).
Saṃvarta:
On the fourth day, the collection of the bones must be performed by the twice-born;
after that collection, the touching of the limbs is prescribed.
[15] On the fourth day for a Brahmin, on the sixth for a Kṣatriya,
and on the eighth and tenth days respectively, there should be contact for a Vaiśya and a Śūdra.
Aṅgiras: During the period of birth-impurity, contact with anyone except the woman who has given birth does not cause defilement;
however, regarding contact with the woman who has given birth, bathing alone is prescribed.
Dakṣa says: "Indeed,
for that brahmin who eats without having bathed, without having offered oblations, and without having given gifts— for such a person, impurity (sūtaka) is declared."
[The time for giving is] never [right] for one who is diseased, miserly, burdened by debt,
devoid of ritual action, foolish, or especially one who is dominated by his wife.
For one whose wealth is addicted to vice, who is perpetually dependent on others,
and who is devoid of faith and renunciation— for such a person, there shall be an end [to his merit] through birth-impurity.
There shall never be a state of non-sūtaka; rather, there is sūtaka for as long as one lives.
Thus, by virtue of this specific quality, it is designated as sūtaka.
[16] In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "In the house of one whose wife has had a previous husband,
there is always impurity regarding all ritual acts, and it persists for as long as she remains in his body."
For him, giving, receiving, and bathing—all shall be in vain.
In these extended injunctions (atideśavākya), the application of the rules for impurity following death (pretaśauca) should be understood to carry over.
Now, regarding impurity on account of birth, Manu [5.61–63] states:
"In the case of a birth, it shall be exactly the same for Brahmins who desire purity."
For all others there is impurity due to death (śāva), but for the mother and father, there is impurity due to birth (sūtaka).
The birth-impurity shall belong to the mother alone; having performed the ritual ablution, the father becomes pure.
But having discharged semen, a man becomes pure simply by touching water;
however, due to the connection arising from seminal emission, he should observe impurity for three days.

“Even so”: just as at death there is impurity characterized by untouchability, so too at birth, for the mother and father alone, there is *sūtaka*—the state of being unfit for touch due to the occasion of childbirth; this is the meaning. “Having touched,” that is, having bathed. “Pure,” meaning fit for touch. [18] Vasiṣṭha and Aṅgiras: “But at birth, the *sūtaka* belongs only to the mother and father. Or rather, it may be exactly thus for Brahmins who desire purity: [it applies] to the mother and father. Some say it belongs to the mother alone because she is the cause of it. Furthermore, they quote:
There is no impurity for a man during childbirth, provided he does not come into contact [with the woman];
it is the menstrual flow that should be known as impure there, and that does not exist in a man.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In the case of birth as well, it is the same for them; therein, both the mother and father are impure. Some say only the mother [is impure]. For the purpose of the *agnihotra* sacrifice, one is pure even after bathing and ritual sipping (*upasparśana*).

Regarding the statement 'at birth, the *sapiṇḍas* are pure,' 'purity' here means fitness for touch, not fitness for performing rituals and so forth, because that would contradict the statements of Hārīta, Devala, Bodhāyana, Viṣṇu, and others. Thus says Hārīta:
"Regarding birth and death, there is a ten-night period of impurity for the family on both sides.
Thus says Devala:
"In birth and in death, impurity invariably follows."
"the sapindas and the maternal relatives," and so forth. Baudhāyana [1.11.1]:
Regarding birth and death, they state that the period of impurity for *sapiṇḍas* lasts ten days.
Thus says Viṣṇu (22.1):
"For a Brāhmaṇa, the period of impurity for his *sapiṇḍas* on account of birth and death is ten days," and so forth.
Śaṅkha states:
"O best of the twice-born, upon birth and death, a sapinda attains purity after ten days," and so forth.

Bṛhaspati [Āśaucakāṇḍa 43]: "Impurity due to death, however, applies to all; impurity due to birth applies to the mother alone. In that case, the father should perform a bath, but the kinsmen need not bathe with their clothes on."
Saṃvarta says:
Even for one who has been born [in such a family], this same rule is observed by the wise:
he shall be purified in ten nights, provided he excludes the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice.
Upon the birth of a son, the father’s bath with his clothes is prescribed;
the mother becomes pure after ten days, but the father may touch her after bathing.
Parāśara [3.27, 25]:
"If a twice-born man seeks contact with his wife after she has given birth,
he shall incur impurity (sūtaka), even if he is a Brahmin learned in the six Vedāṅgas."
[20] However, upon a birth, a twice-born householder should not cause a mixture of funeral rites;
the mother becomes pure after ten days, while the father is purified by bathing.
"Contact" means physical touch. This is according to the statement of Saṃvarta: "But regarding the birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) of a mother, it applies to one who touches her, and not to others.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Upon the birth of a child, the father, having seen the face [of the newborn]..."
Having performed a bath with one's clothes on, one becomes pure at that very moment.
And if other mothers likewise do not enter that house,
then even the sapindas should always be sent away, even if they are in close proximity.
A Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, or a Vaiśyā woman who has given birth becomes touchable after ten days have passed;
however, a Śūdrā woman becomes touchable after thirteen days.
Bṛhatpracetā says:
A woman who has given birth becomes pure after ten days, regardless of her caste.
Paiṭhīnasi:

One should have a woman who has given birth to a son bathe after twenty nights and then have her perform all ritual acts; a woman who has given birth to a daughter, after one month. Thus ends the impurity due to childbirth.
[21] 3 Now, the rules concerning birth and death.
Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"The father, the grandfather, and likewise the great-grandfather are born again on that very day, and they make it known."
Therefore, that day is meritorious and increases the prosperity of the ancestors; by merely remembering one's forefathers, that day does not become defiled.
Hārīta:

"When a son is born, because of the joy of the ancestors, that day is meritorious. Therefore, having invited Brahmins, one should offer the *svadhā* to the ancestors with vessels full of sesame seeds and gold. And until the severing of the umbilical cord, they perform for the person the purificatory rites intended for merit. But once the umbilical cord is severed, [the period of] impurity begins."—Manu.
On the day a son is born,
one may freely accept gifts of gold, grain, cattle, clothing, sesame seeds, food, molasses, and clarified butter.

[22] Śaṅkha and Likhita state: Upon the birth of a son, while the umbilical cord remains uncut, there is no restriction even on accepting gifts of molasses, sesame, oil, gold, clothing, upper garments, cows, and grain. Now, regarding purification, this applies to two-footed and four-footed animals, grain, and sacrificial fees.
Paiṭhīnasi says:

In the matter of giving and receiving, there is no fault in making a distinction such as "gold" or "cows. Now, regarding the section on purity, Kāśyapa says: A Brāhmaṇa should not accept [gifts] from those [outcastes] even with his hand; he should not take them, except for two-footed or four-footed animals, grain, and gold.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Salt, honey, meat, flowers, roots, and fruits;
wood, clods of earth, grass, leaves, as well as curd, milk, and ghee."
Medicinal herbs, oil, a hide, sour gruel, and food may always be accepted from the house of those who are impure; likewise, one may take merchandise and roots that have been offered for sale.
On this point, Jābāli says:

"The twilight prayers, the five great sacrifices, the daily rites, and the duties prescribed by the Smṛtis—one should suspend these during that period of impurity; their performance resumes again at the end of ten days."
Śaṅkha says:

One should suspend giving, receiving gifts, burnt offerings, Vedic study, and rites for the ancestors during a period of impurity, with the exception of the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for the deceased.
[23] And in the case of a human [death]: for ten days in both cases, the food of the household is not eaten;
giving, receiving, burnt offerings, and Vedic recitation are suspended.
"In both cases" refers to birth and death impurity (*sūtaka-mṛtaka*). The mention of "ten days" is an indicative mark for the period of ritual impurity (*aśauca*).
Kātyāyana states in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [Gobhila 3.60–63]:
"In the case of birth-impurity, the abandonment of rituals such as the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*) is prescribed."
The Homa sacrifice, however, must be performed according to the Śrauta rites, even with dry food or fruits.
One should cause the *akṛta* (unprepared) to be offered in the *smārta* rite; in its absence, the *kṛtākṛta* (half-prepared).
Why [is it said] "one should cause to be offered"? Because of the injunction not dependent on a specific context (*anārabhyavidhi*).
Prepared food such as rice-meal and the like, and rice-grains and the like which are both prepared and unprepared,
as well as unprepared grains such as paddy— thus is the sacrificial offering declared by the wise to be of three kinds.
In cases of birth-impurity, while traveling abroad, or when unable to eat at a śrāddha,
one should apply the rule "or he should cause [the rite] to be offered" in the presence of such and other similar circumstances.

“Regarding ‘one should cause [the sacrifice] to be offered’ (hāvayet), what is the scope? and so forth—by asking “what is the scope of that which is prescribed beginning with the domestic fire (gṛha-agni)?”, he states the specific scope by means of the passage beginning with “during impurity (sūtaka) and during menstruation (pravrāsa)” [Pāraskara 3.10.31–34]: “They should not recite their Vedic study (svādhyāya). Obligatory rites (nitya) should be suspended, with the exception of those pertaining to the sacrificial fires (vaitāna). Some say they should also be suspended for the domestic fire (śālāgni). Others should perform these [rites].”

“Vaitāna” refers to the rites of the Śrauta fires. “In the domestic fire” (śālāgni) means in the Smārta fire; excluding that, some teachers desire the cessation [of ritual duties] even in the domestic fire. Because of the expression “some,” Karka maintains that when there is cessation by one person, then others should perform these acts and not oneself. Yama says:
“Manu has declared that during a period of birth-impurity (sūtaka), the food of the family is without fault.”
On the eleventh day, one should perform acts of giving, study, and austerity.
This is said to him who follows the practice of the obstruction of dharma in three ways:
the fire produced from the fire-drills shall always burn away the evil that has been committed.

Regarding the statement, “The food of a family during *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) is faultless”—this is said for the purpose of removing the threefold obstruction to *dharma* that arises when one who is in a state of *sūtaka* lacks the means to give gifts. For this very reason, it is stated [in the *Tantrāloka*]: “Fire produced from the two kindling-sticks (*araṇī*)... and so forth. Manu [5.84] says:
“One should not prolong the days of impurity, nor should one interrupt the ritual procedures involving the sacred fires.”
And while performing that rite, even a close relative does not become impure.

“‘One should not increase the days of impurity’—the meaning is that one whose restriction of impurity is based on considerations such as livelihood should not prolong the days of impurity with the thought, ‘He who is free from ritual duties will remain at ease. ‘*Paryūhaḥ*’ means rejection. ‘And not,’ etc.—just as a sacrificer performing the fire-ritual does not become impure, so too one who has bathed is not impure when performing that ritual. Jābāli says: “Upon birth or death, there is no abandonment of ritual duties for one who maintains the sacrificial canopy (*vitāna*).”
The oblation must indeed be performed exclusively in the domestic fire by those born of other lineages.
In both cases, the period of impurity for the sapinda relatives lasts ten days;
by the repeated practice of ritual bathing and touching water, they become fit for the performance of the Agnihotra sacrifice.
Now, the impurity resulting from the contact of castes.
In that regard, Dakṣa says:
"When there is only one husband for women of the various castes according to the natural order of classes,
the birth-impurity (sūtaka) shall last ten days, six days, three days, or one day, respectively."
Hārīta states: A Brāhmaṇa becomes pure in ten days upon the birth or death of a member of his own caste;
however, he becomes pure in seven, five, or three nights upon the birth or death of one belonging to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes respectively.

For a Brāhmaṇa, among Sapiṇḍas who are Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, the periods are six nights, three nights, and one night respectively. For a Kṣatriya, among Vaiśyas and Śūdras, they are six nights and three nights. For a Vaiśya, among Śūdras, it is six nights. (Brahmapurāṇa)
And for a Brahmin, when kinsmen belonging to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya,
or Śūdra castes have died or been born, purification is held to occur after ten days.
Because local custom is an authority, there is a six-night period for Kṣatriyas,
three nights for Vaiśyas, and one day for Śūdras.
[27] Furthermore, when a Kṣatriya dies, or a Vaiśya, or likewise a Śūdra who is a relative of a Vaiśya, one should observe one's own period of impurity in that case.
Śūdras, Vaiśyas, and Kṣatriyas move among the higher castes in their respective order among their kinsmen, according to the number [of generations] that exists among them.
Śaṅkha [18.17–20]: For Śūdra sapindas, the period of impurity for the social classes is traditionally recorded as one night, three nights, six nights, and one month, respectively.
For a Vaiśya who is a sapinda, the period of impurity for the [other] castes is traditionally recorded as three nights, six nights, a fortnight, and likewise a month, respectively.
For a Kṣatriya who is a sapinda, the purification for a Brāhmaṇa is six nights;
for the remaining castes, one should prescribe twelve days.
"Regarding a Brāhmaṇa who is a sapinda, all castes without distinction shall become pure after ten nights; thus said you, Yama."
Aṅgiras said:
The sons of twice-born men born of women of a different caste are proclaimed to have distinct religious practices and are declared to have distinct rules of purification.
The son of a Śūdra woman born from a Brāhmaṇa is called a Pāraśava;
for him as well, the rules of purity and impurity are prescribed according to the conduct of a Śūdra.
[28] Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

If many who are born of one [father] have separate fields, separate houses, and a single funeral cake (piṇḍa), they have separate purifications; however, the funeral cake extends through three generations.
Jābāli says:

Among various castes, one should know that for a living father, the property belongs to the paternal line; when the father has passed away, it belongs to the maternal line; but in the case of others, it belongs to both.

For wives and slaves, the period of impurity is equal to that of their master according to their respective order of birth (ānulomya). When the master has died, they are purified by their own period of impurity. For those of lower caste, in the case of sapinda relatives of a higher caste, purification occurs upon the expiration of the latter's period of impurity.
Bṛhaspati [Āśauca 35]:
Slaves, apprentices, hired servants, and pupils living together with their master are purified by the same degree of ritual purity as the master in cases of death or birth-impurity.
Śaṅkha says:
But if a virtuous woman of low caste should give birth through negligence,
the impurity pertaining to that birth does not cease at the time of delivery or death.
Thus concludes the impurity resulting from the contact between castes.
Now, regarding the concurrence of periods of impurity (āśauca): on this point, Manu [5.89] states:
"If another death or birth should occur within the ten-day period..."
A Brahmin shall remain impure for as long as that period of ten days has not yet elapsed.
Yājñavalkya [3.20]: Between birth and death, one is purified by the remaining days. Baudhāyana [1.11.15–16]:

When there is a coincidence of birth and death, the period of impurity is ten nights. Now, if several periods of ten nights should coincide, the impurity lasts for the first ten-night period until the ninth day. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "If, however, someone should die or be born in the interval, one becomes pure by the remaining days alone; if it occurs when a day remains, purification is by two days; if at dawn, by three days."

Gautama [14.6–8]: If that [impurity] recurs within the period, they shall be purified by the remainder [of the original term]. If it occurs during the remainder of a night, purification is by two days; if at dawn, by three days. The same applies to the death of a relative occurring during a period of impurity due to a death. Aṅgiras:

If another birth-impurity occurs during an existing birth-impurity before ten days have passed, purification shall occur by the remainder of that first period; the same applies when a death-impurity occurs during a birth-impurity.
If, within ten days of a birth, a death should subsequently occur,
the relatives must observe the period of impurity for that deceased person.

[31] Devala: When the duration of impurity increases, purification is prescribed for each successive period beyond that. However, if it occurs on or after the fifth day, one is also instructed to follow the rule of the preceding period.
When multiple impurities occur simultaneously, purification should be understood as being determined by the more serious one;
however, when death and birth coincide, death shall be considered the weightier factor.
Śaṅkha says: "Indeed, one should conclude the purification that is common [to all] with the first [rite];
that which is not common [to all] with the second, according to the word of Dharmarāja."
Yama states: "In the event of an increase in sin (or a birth), one should conclude the period of impurity according to the latter [period]. This is also stated in the *Brahma Purāṇa*.
As long as the first two parts of the birth-impurity (sūtaka) have not elapsed during a birth-impurity,
purification is held to occur from the end of the first impurity once the second has fallen away.
From this point forward, one is considered pure after the second period of birth-impurity (sūtaka);
in the same way, this should be understood regarding death-impurity (mṛtaka) when another death-impurity occurs.
Whatever impurity of birth (sūtaka) occurs within an impurity of death (mṛtaka), or where an impurity of death occurs within an impurity of birth; [in such cases, the later impurity shall prevail].
At the end of the funeral rites, there shall always be [such a person] among the four castes.
[32] 6 Now, impurity for those residing abroad.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati [Āśauca 36.62] states:
"This summary of the essence of impurity has been proclaimed for when one is in close proximity;
it is declared that when a death or birth occurs in a distant land, purification is immediate."
Upon hearing that a kinsman has died in another country, or that a son has been born,
one becomes pure after the remaining days of the ten-day period have passed.

Pāraskara [3.10.44–45]: If one who has gone abroad should die, those who have already offered the water-libations shall remain for the remainder of the period; if he has been deceased for longer than that, they shall remain for one night or three nights. Manu [5.75–78]:
If one hears that a person who has gone abroad has died within ten days,
he shall remain impure only for as long as remains of those ten nights.
If ten days have passed, one shall remain impure for three nights;
but once a year has elapsed, one becomes pure simply by touching water.
Upon hearing of the death of a kinsman or the birth of a son after the ten-day period has passed,
a person becomes pure by immersing himself in water along with his clothes.
"Passed away" means destroyed. "Less than ten days" means within ten days having not yet elapsed. Yājñavalkya [3.21]:
"If he has gone abroad, the period shall be the remainder of the time; once it is complete, one becomes pure after offering water."
Vasiṣṭha [3.36]:
If one hears of a deceased person who was residing in another country after ten days have passed, the period of impurity lasts for one night. Gautama [14.18]: [The same].
And having heard [of the birth], after the tenth day, there is the *pakṣiṇī* period.
The tenth night is that which pertains to the connection with the *sūtaka* (impurity). A *pakṣiṇī* is a night joined by the preceding and following days.

Upon hearing [of a birth or death] while residing in another country, one becomes pure through the remainder of the period of impurity (*āśauca*) regarding birth and death. However, if the period of impurity has already elapsed, one becomes pure after one night at the end of the year; beyond that, by means of a bath. Jābāla says:
"When the *sūtaka* has passed, there shall be a three-night *sūtaka* for each respective case."
But when a full year has passed, immediate purification is prescribed.
Devala says:
If, after the days of impurity have passed, one hears that a kinsman has died within the course of a year,
there shall be three nights of impurity in that case.
If it is heard that a person has died more than half a year ago, [the impurity] here shall last for only one day; however, this does not apply to renunciants (saṃnyāsins).

There is no impurity (*āśauca*) regarding a birth even when the days have passed; "within a year" means within the interval of one year. Herein is the established rule: upon hearing of the death of a relative within six months, there is impurity for three nights; beyond that, up to three months, it is for a "two-day period" (*pakṣiṇī*); beyond that, up to three months, it is for one night; after this, there is merely the requirement of bathing and the offering of water. [35]
Now, regarding impurity (āśauca) due to the death of a child and others,
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

In the case of a child who has died in a foreign land or has passed away, purification is immediate; some say this applies if the child was less than two years old and had not yet developed teeth. Paiṭhīnasi states:
"For one who has died in a foreign land, purification is immediate."
Vaivasvata said:
"In the case of a child who has not yet cut its teeth, the impurity due to death lasts three nights;
'there is immediate purity,' so says Gautama."
When a child, one residing in another country, or a person belonging to a different lineage (pṛthakpiṇḍa) has died,
one becomes pure immediately by plunging into water with one's clothes on.
[36] For men whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed, impurity is prescribed to last for one night;
but for those whose tonsure has been completed, purification is held to occur after three nights.
“An infant (*bāla*)” here refers to one who has not yet cut his teeth; “one who is a separate funeral ball (*pṛthakpiṇḍa*)” here refers to one for whom the water-rites (*samānodaka*) have ceased.
Yama says: “In the case of an infant less than three years old, the state of a ghost (*pretatva*) follows.”
Likewise, when a son has not yet grown teeth, or when he is an infant, or when a miscarriage occurs;
If a young boy who has undergone the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā) dies while traveling to another country,
all his sapinda relatives must observe a period of impurity for one day and night.
Yājñavalkya [3.23]: For those who have not yet cut their teeth, purification is immediate; until the *cūḍā* ceremony, it is held to be one night;
until the initiation (*vratādeśa*), it is three nights; and beyond that, ten nights.
Jābāla says: For the twice-born, in the case of those who have died while observing vows or after the tonsure ceremony,
they are purified in ten days, three days, or one day respectively— even if they were devoid of virtues.

“Vrata” refers to the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*). Viṣṇu [22.27–31]: In the case of a child who has died before the eruption of teeth, the purification is immediate; for such a child there is neither cremation with fire nor the water libation. However, if the teeth have erupted but the tonsure (*cūḍā*) has not been performed, purification occurs after one day and night. If the tonsure has been performed but the initiation has not yet taken place, it is after three nights. Beyond that, it is according to the time prescribed for each respective stage.
[37] Śaṅkha says: For a child who has not yet cut its teeth, immediate purification is prescribed;
likewise, purification occurs after one day and night for a child whose tonsure ceremony (cūḍā) has not been performed.
In the same way, however, if [the child] has not been initiated (*anupanīta*), the kinsmen become pure after three days.
Here, "those whose teeth have not yet emerged" and so forth are indicative of their respective time-periods. Paiṭhīnasi says:
For those whose tonsure ceremony has not been performed, the period of impurity lasts three nights.
Vasiṣṭha [4.34–35] states:
"When a child less than two years old dies, or in the case of a miscarriage, the impurity for the sapindas lasts three nights; according to Gautama, however, it is immediate purification."
In this regard, the distinction between the object burned and the burner is as stated by Aṅgiras:
"But for one who has not yet been born [or] for one who has passed away,
there shall be impurity only so long as the kinsmen do not perform their ablutions with their clothes on outside."
Even if he has not had his tonsure ceremony performed and has not yet cut his teeth, should he pass away,
one should nevertheless cremate him and observe impurity for three days.

“Unborn” means one whose teeth have not yet emerged. [Pāraskara 3.10.2–6]: When a child under two years of age dies, the impurity (āśauca) belongs to the mother and father; for others, it is purity (śauca) alone. [The period of impurity] is one night or three nights. Without cremating the body, they bury it. If the death occurs during a birth-impurity (sūtaka), the impurity lasts until the end of the birth-impurity period.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "One who has not yet reached two years of age, having died, should be laid upon the ground;
the impurity for his relatives shall last for two nights in every respect."
But where even a deceased person who has not yet passed two years is cremated,
that place becomes similar to [the cremation grounds] due to excessive delusion and other spirits, as well as from the commonality of the region and its softness.
For Brahmins, however, impurity lasts for three nights and does not extend further;
for Kshatriyas it lasts eleven days, and for Vaishyas it lasts twelve days.
[39] Furthermore, for Śūdras, it shall be twenty nights in due order;
likewise, an uninitiated Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya who has not yet taken up the bow [shall observe the same].
Wherever a Vaiśya who has not grasped the whip, or a Śūdra who is still clad in his garment,
dies, there the period of impurity shall indeed be only three days.
This period of six years applies to the three twice-born castes;
for Śūdras, it is five years, after which the duties prescribed for their own respective classes follow.
[40] 8 Now, regarding the impurity of women.
In this regard, following the rule that "relatives are purified after three days," Śaṅkha states:
"But for unmarried girls of Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and the twice-born [castes],
and for a Śūdra who has not yet taken a wife, [the impurity lasts] beyond sixteen years."
If death occurs within that month, his kinsmen shall attain purification; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Likewise: "In the same way, for three days [is the impurity] when daughters die or are given away while still in the house. — Manu 5.72.
In the case of women who have not undergone the sacramental rites, the kinsmen become pure after three days;
however, the uterine relatives become pure according to the very rule already stated.

"Of those who are unprepared" means those who have been verbally betrothed but for whom the marriage has not yet been performed. "Relatives" (*bāndhavāḥ*) refers to the *sapindas* of the husband; "kinsmen" (*sanābhayaḥ*) refers to the *sapindas* of the father.
[41] Yājñavalkya [3.24]: "But for unmarried girls and for boys, purification occurs after one day."

Marriage is the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) for women. Among women who have undergone this rite, there is no impurity on the paternal side; however, if their birth or death occurs in the father’s house, then there shall be one night or three nights of impurity.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "When a maiden has been married, there is an end to the lineage, the funeral cakes, and the impurity after one day. Vasiṣṭha [4.19] says:
A maiden who has been given away becomes another's. Śaṅkha says: A woman who sees her menses while still in her father’s house and remains unconsecrated [by marriage]...
When she has died, the period of impurity never ceases at any time.
[42] In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "A woman given away from her father’s house— whether she gives birth or dies while residing in the primary [household]—
should properly observe her own period of impurity while established in a separate place."
If a girl dies anywhere from birth until the time of the tonsure ceremony (cūḍā),
there shall always be immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca) for all castes.
Therefore, up until the giving of the bride in marriage, it is indeed only for one day;
beyond this, for those who have reached adulthood, the settled rule is three nights.
When the formal betrothal has been performed there, it should be understood that for three days the status belongs to both [the father and the groom];
thereafter, for those who have been given away, it belongs to the husband alone.
[43] The period of impurity for birth or death shall be as prescribed by one's own caste;
however, a maiden who, having been given away by her father, has out of independence resorted to another man [is not subject to this].
Whomever she has resorted to again, for that person there shall be impurity for three days, whether she has died or given birth; such is the settled rule, and not for others.
But when she has been given away at the seventh [step], if she has become a maiden, her lineage shall be that of her husband; and that is further distinguished.
But if she has not given birth, her [sons] belong to her father; thereafter, they belong to her former husband.
If, however, out of desire, she has gone to another while still a virgin and remains with him, [the sons belong to that other].
She would become a kinswoman of that other man whom she herself had taken as her refuge.
Now, regarding the impurity resulting from a miscarriage.
On this point, Manu says (7.66):
"In the case of a miscarriage, she becomes pure after as many nights as there were months;
when her menses have ceased, a virtuous woman who has become menstruating is purified by bathing."
Hārīta [Ācār.

19]: In the case of a miscarriage among women, there is impurity for three nights; this is because it is more significant due to the specific nature of the menstrual flow. If a child is born dead or dies shortly after birth, the family remains impure for ten days and so forth.
Śaṅkha and Likhita:
The period of impurity following a miscarriage lasts for as many nights as there were months of gestation, or for three days. This applies to all members of the family.
Śātātapa states: "In the case of a miscarriage, the impurity lasts for three nights; or for as many days as there were months."
In the continuation of the word "purity," Viṣṇu [22.27] states: "In the case of a miscarriage, [the penance lasts for] as many days and nights as there were months [of pregnancy]. Jābāla says:

The nights [of impurity] for the mother following the miscarriage of the fetus shall be equal to the months [of pregnancy]. Sumantu states: "The days [of impurity] for the miscarriage of the fetus are equal to the months of the pregnancy; or else, there is immediate purification."
[In the Kūrma Purāṇa: If a miscarriage should occur within six months,
then their purification is prescribed by days equal in number to those months.
From this point forward, the impurity prescribed for their own respective classes is ordained for them;
however, in the case of a miscarriage, immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca) is required for the sapindas.
[In the Ādipurāṇa: For women, however, a fallen embryo, or one born and then immediately dead,
or one who dies before the eruption of teeth, or after six months have passed since being brought outside [the womb], [is not subject to the same rites].
Having adorned it with garments and other ornaments, one should deposit it like a piece of wood;
having dug slowly into the earth, immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca) is prescribed.
Now, the specific impurity resulting from death.
In that context, with the phrase "immediate purification is ordained" recurring, Manu [5.95] states:
"And for those killed in a riotous battle, by lightning, or by the king;
for one who has died for the sake of cows or Brahmins; and for whomever the king so desires."
Yama states:
"Immediate purification is ordained for those killed by a thunderbolt or a child, as well as for those who sacrifice their lives, and for those [killed] by rivers, kings, or fanged beasts."
But for him who fights facing the enemy according to the rules of weaponry as prescribed by the treatises, his sacrifice is perfected; for him, immediate purification is ordained.

Immediate purification is ordained for those who have entered the fire, those who have leaped from Mount Meru, those on the path of heroes, those who have practiced fasting unto death, and for all who have been initiated.

Bṛhaspati [Āśaucakāṇḍa 45]: "In cases other than a riot, for those killed by lightning, by the king, or while protecting cows or Brahmins, the great seers declare immediate purification; others, however, say three days."
Parāśara: For those who perish for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, for those killed by a magistrate, for those killed while recovering stolen cattle,
and for those who perish in battles, there is one night of impurity.

For those killed by cows or Brahmins, purification is immediate (*anvakṣam*). Also for those killed through the king's wrath or in battle; and for those who desire it by means of fasting (*prāya*), self-destruction (*nāśaka*), weapons, fire, poison, water, hanging, or falling from a precipice.
"Purification" here means immediate purification. "Fasting" (*prāya*) refers to walking along a great highway.
Śaṅkha says:
There is no period of impurity for those who kill themselves by means of a cliff, fire, fasting, or water;
nor for those who have fallen [from their caste], nor for those killed by weapons or lightning.
If one should cause his own death by himself through means such as poison, fire, water, or the like,
no period of impurity is prescribed for him, nor is there to be the offering of fire or the libation of water.
Now, if someone should die through negligence in fire, water, or similar circumstances,
the period of impurity must be observed for him, and the water-libation rite must be performed for him.
Sumantu:

For those who die in a battle involving Bhṛgu, fire, or water, or in a foreign land, or from lightning or a great noise, the water-rites (udakakriyā) should be performed; there is immediate purification (sadyaḥśauca).
Regarding the phrase "immediate purification," Śaṅkha and Likhita state this as a continuation [of the rule].
Now, the same applies even to execution by means of weapons, starvation, fire, poison, a thunderbolt, Bhṛgu, water, or serpents. Jābāla says:
"In times of famine, during a national calamity, or when one has been killed by weapons, cows, or Brahmins..."
Nor when [the husband] has fallen from caste, is dead, has gone abroad, or is impotent.
The meaning is that there is no period of impurity for these [persons]. Hārīta states:
"For those who have died by jumping into fire, by Mount Meru, or by lions, tigers, children, or in battle, there is immediate purification."

Kāśyapa states: For those who have died by fasting, those struck by lightning, those who have entered fire or water, those who have died during the change of seasons, in battle, or while traveling to another country, as well as for fetuses and those who die after teeth have emerged, purification occurs after three nights.
[In the] Brahma Purāṇa:
Even a man afflicted by great diseases that are difficult to cure may enter a blazing fire or likewise practice fasting unto death.
One should also go with devotion to the fathomless mass of waters, to the very fall of Bhṛgu,
to the Great Path (Mahāpatha), or to the Snowy Mountain (Tuṣāragiri).
Or, when the time has arrived, the high-minded one may effect the abandonment of the body from the tip of a branch of the banyan tree at Prayāga, by means of his own bodily dissolution.
[50] One who commits suicide might sometimes attain the highest worlds;
one who performs great sinful deeds enjoys divine pleasures in heaven.
The entitlement to these ascetic practices belongs at all times to all living beings—
both men and women, and across all social classes.
For those among the living for whom such a corpse might exist anywhere,
their period of impurity shall be three days, as it is likewise when one is struck by a thunderbolt or fire.
[51] 11 Now, the impurity for those not related by sapinda-connection.
In this regard, Manu and Viṣṇu state:
"A disciple, however, should perform the funeral rites (pitṛmedha) for his deceased teacher;
he becomes purified there by a period of ten nights together with those who carry the corpse."
The *pitṛmedha* is the funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*). According to Āśvalāyana [4.5.4–9]:

For ten days, one should avoid giving gifts and studying among *sapiṇḍa* relatives, as well as for a teacher who is not a *sapiṇḍa*. For unmarried women, the period is three nights; likewise for other teachers, and for a *jñāti* who is not a *sapiṇḍa*. For married women, the period is one day, provided they have not yet reached puberty or have already given birth. The same applies for a fellow student (*sabrahmacārin*) and for a *śrotriya* residing in the same village.

[52] Gautama [14.18–27]: Having heard [of a death], for three days after the tenth day; for a non-*sapiṇḍa* relative connected by birth, and for a fellow student; for one who has lived the life of a religious student (*sabrahmacārin*), for one day; and for a *śrotriya* who has arrived. Upon touching a corpse, if it was done intentionally, there is impurity for ten nights. This has been stated regarding Vaiśyas and Śūdras, and for the two preceding classes (Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas). Or, for three days. And the same applies to the teacher, his son, his wife, one for whom he performs sacrifices, and his pupil. Manu [5.80–82, 71]:
When a teacher has passed away, they say that the period of impurity lasts for three nights;
likewise, when his son or his wife dies, the rule is that it lasts for one day and night.

Upon the death of a learned Śrotriya who has been received as a guest, one shall remain impure for three nights; likewise for a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman, the impurity lasts for a period of two nights and the intervening day.
When the king has died, one who resides within his realm must remain impure for as long as the light [of the sun or stars] lasts;
however, if it is a non-Vedic king, the impurity lasts for a full day, and likewise if it is a teacher who is well-versed in the Vedas.
[53] It is ordained that for a fellow celibate student (sabrahmacārin), purification occurs after one day has passed;
however, for those who share the same funeral water (ekodaka) in birth, purification is held to occur after three nights.
“Until the light [of the stars]” means until the appearance of the constellations. Śaṅkha says: “When the maternal grandfather has likewise passed away, or when the teacher has likewise died...”
When daughters die in the house, or likewise when they have been given away in marriage, [the impurity lasts] for three days.
When the king who was their resident has died, and likewise when a daughter's son is born,
or when the teacher’s wife and sons have died, [the impurity lasts] for one day.
One should observe a fast for three nights upon the death of a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, or a kinsman;
likewise, one should observe a fast for one day upon the death of a fellow student or a person who has studied the Veda with him.

Yājñavalkya [3.24]: For maidens whose hand has not been given away, for children, for the teacher’s pupil, for one who has studied the Vedas under him, for a maternal uncle, and for a learned Śrotriya, purification occurs within a day.
Bṛhaspati [Āśauc. 27.33]: A man becomes pure after three days in the case of a maternal grandfather, a teacher, and a Śrotriya;
in the case of a maternal uncle, a pupil, an officiating priest, and a kinsman, it is a night with its two surrounding days (pakṣiṇī).
But if one dies who is not learned in the Vedas, the impurity lasts for a full day; likewise if it is a teacher;
and if a king dies whose subjects reside within his realm, it lasts as long as the light [of the sun or moon].
Baudhāyana says: "One should observe it for three nights, a day and a night, or for one day. Jābāla says: [the same].

For those related by water (samānodaka), the impurity lasts for three days; for those born of the same lineage (gotraja), it is remembered as one day; and likewise for a maternal relative, a teacher, a friend, and a regional ruler.
In the continuation of the phrase "one shall be purified," Viṣṇu states (22.42–45):
"When the preceptor or the maternal grandfather has passed away, purification occurs after three nights;
likewise when non-aurasa sons are born or when they have died."
When wives who have had previous husbands have given birth or have died;

In the case of the death of the teacher’s wife, a son, a sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, a brother-in-law, a fellow student, or a pupil, one must observe impurity for one night. This also applies to the king of one's own country.
"Brother-in-law" (*śvaśurya*) means a sister's husband. Thus says Hārīta.

In the case of wives who have had previous husbands, of deceased sons, and of one's maternal grandfather, the period of impurity shall be three nights; however, for those related through the sapinda connection, it is one day.
Yājñavalkya [3.25]: In the case of non-aurasa sons, wives who have gone to others, and when a king or a resident has died, that very day is the cause for purification.
[55] In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: "Excepting the legitimate son (*aurasa*), among sons born of wives of equal caste at all times— whether they have been born or have died— "
And the period of impurity shall be three nights for those who share the same lineage; this is the settled rule.
Likewise: "If, at the outset, a girl has been betrothed to one [man] but [subsequently] given to another, [the impurity lasts] for two sons..."
Where there is a three-night period for the father, there it shall be one night for the sapindas.
Where there is one mother for two [sons], and two fathers in some cases,
there should be a unity of impurity (*sūtaka*) between them either from the birth or from the day of death.
Śaṅkha says:
"In the case of sons other than those born of one's own body, wives who have gone to another man,
and women who have had previous husbands, purification is held to occur after three nights."
Bṛhaspati [Āśaucakāṇḍa 24]: "In the case of wives who have had previous husbands, or in the case of the wives of others,
and when they have died, the best of the twice-born becomes pure after bathing and observing a three-night period of impurity."
In the continuation of the term “impurity,” Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

“In the case of wives who have had previous husbands, and in the case of sons [born of such wives], when they die, there is impurity for three days; during that time, there is neither study nor the performance of water-libation rites.”
impurity resulting from removal and so forth.
Regarding this, Manu (5.100–103) says:
"O best of the twice-born, this purification among sapinda relatives has been declared to you.
Now learn the purification for the dead among all those who are not sapindas."
Having carried out the corpse of a deceased twice-born man who is not a sapinda, a Brahmin becomes pure after three nights, as does one who carries out the kinsmen on his mother's side.
If one eats their food, however, one is purified in ten days;
if one does not eat their food, one is purified in a single day, provided one does not dwell in that house.
If one does not wish to attend a funeral, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter, whether the deceased kinsman is related or unrelated.

"Like a kinsman" means out of affection or the like, as if toward a relative, for the sake of a visible purpose. In that case, for one who eats and resides [with the family], the period lasts ten nights; for one who resides but does not eat, it lasts three nights; and for one who neither resides nor eats, it lasts one night. Aṅgiras says:
"But having eaten within the ten-day period during a birth-impurity (sūtaka) or even a death-impurity (mṛtaka)..."
He shall remain untouchable for as long as he performs that vow.
[57] In the case of birth-impurity or death-impurity, the impurity relating to a corpse lasts until the collection of the bones;
for those engaged in a continuous feast of food, raw grain is forbidden as food.
Having eaten their cooked food, one should drink only milk for three nights.
Starting from the beginning, however, the other [the mourner] should eat only in the evening and not in between;
he shall become pure together with his sapinda relatives by sleeping on the ground and remaining well-restrained.
But that person of any caste who eats during the period of impurity of another shall also become impure;
the wise have declared that his purification likewise occurs at the end of that same period.

Regarding the eating [of food] within ten days of one who is not a *sapiṇḍa*, this [rule] concerning "touchability" (*saṃspṛśyatva*) should be understood. "That vow" (*tadvratam*) refers to the observance of the rules for that period of impurity (*āśauca*), not a penance (*prāyaścitta*). "Funeral rites" (*śāvam*) refers to the actions occasioned by death, such as carrying the funeral bier (*kaṭadhāraṇa*) and so forth.
Bṛhaspati [states]:
"He who, even though not a *sapiṇḍa*, should share a bed or a seat with those [impure persons]... [Āśauca 44].
Whether a kinsman or even a non-kinsman, one becomes pure after ten days.
"If someone who is not a sapinda dies in anyone's house by any means whatsoever, that person's impurity should be known to last for three nights; there is no doubt in this matter."
[58] If one unintentionally eats the food of a deceased person for whom one is not a sapinda,
there shall be impurity for three days in every case, even for those who are not sapindas.
In the context of the recurring phrase "one becomes pure in one night," Viṣṇu [22.46] states: "And when someone who is not a sapinda dies in one's own house. Paiṭhīnasi says: [text follows].
Having abandoned a non-relative twice-born man, there is immediate purification; in the case of a relative, it is three nights. Baudhāyana [1.11.30–32]:

Upon touching the corpse of another, if unintentionally, one becomes pure immediately after touching water while wearing one's clothes; if intentionally, it is three nights. And so too in the case of a woman in her menses.
Yājñavalkya [3.14]: Even for those who have touched a corpse, the rites beginning with the entry [into the village] are performed;
for those who so desire, purification occurs instantly, while for others it comes through bathing and self-restraint.
Aṅgiras: If anyone who is not a sapinda should somehow carry out the cremation of a deceased person,
he becomes pure on that very day by bathing with his clothes on and touching fire.
[59] Parāśara [3.41]: Those twice-born who first carry a Brahmin who is without a protector obtain,
step by step, the fruit of a sacrifice in its proper sequence.
A Brāhmaṇa is not defiled by touching a corpse or by the funeral rites;
whether he is the carrier or the one who provides the fire, he becomes pure immediately after bathing.
[In the *Kūrmapurāṇa*]:
If an inferior person touches a superior caste, or if a superior person touches an inferior one,
out of affection while in a state of impurity, he becomes pure through that same period of impurity.
Parāśara [3.47]: A Brāhmaṇa who, weak in knowledge, follows a Śūdra who has become a corpse as it is being carried away, shall remain impure for three nights.

Vasiṣṭha: Having touched human bone that is oily (moist), there is impurity for three nights; but if it is not oily, it is for one day and night. The same applies to following a corpse. [In the Brahmapurāṇa (Ādipurāṇa):]
If a man should carry away a woman of a different caste by paying her price and then cremate her,
his period of impurity shall always be equal to that of the deceased's own class.

[60] All castes become impure for three days after cremating a member of their own caste; however, after carrying out the funeral of one belonging to another caste, they become impure according to the rules of that other caste.
Having cremated a person of their own caste who is not a sapinda relative, those fools who eat at that person's house undergo the period of impurity prescribed for their own caste.
Those who eat food given after cremating one who died of another caste are declared to be contemptible men; they partake in that period of impurity.
Having cremated the deceased teacher by paying his fee, the student’s period of impurity shall be ten nights; this is the settled rule.
Having himself burned an ācārya, an upādhyāya, a guru, a father, or a mother, one who is observing a vow may eat there.
Having done so, he falls; therefore, one should not eat the food of such a person.
One should take food elsewhere and should not dwell together with them.
Having become impure for one day, he becomes pure on the second day. Likewise:
A Brāhmaṇa should not cremate a Śūdra, whether he be a friend or anyone else.
Having burned [the body] out of delusion, one should then bathe, touch fire, and consume clarified butter.
[61] One who is devoted to fasting becomes pure after three nights;
for all [others], there shall be purification after one day and night, even from following a corpse.
The procedure for sounds and touch prescribed by rule is ordained for all castes,
as long as the bones of the deceased Brāhmaṇa have not even been collected.
In that case, whoever is a kinsman who cries out there along with the kinsmen of the deceased, his purification occurs through bathing; thereafter, sipping water (ācamana) is prescribed.
If a Brahmin wails over the funeral pyre of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya before the collection of the bones has occurred,
he becomes pure by bathing with his clothes on on the second day.
After the collection of the bones, one becomes pure after a day and night;
for others, purification occurs by bathing with one's clothes on, even if the collection of the bones has not yet been performed.
But for those born as Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, bathing alone is prescribed when the [five] fires have been established.
[62] 13 Now, those who are not subject to impurity (anāśaucin).
Regarding this, Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"The king is the source of dharma for all; therefore, he is not obstructed by the defects that produce ghosts. Thus it is said:
"The king's domestic priest is to be honored; his purity arises from that [the king's] support."
But a disciple does not transfer his paternal purity to his teacher.
But the funeral rice-ball and the water-offering go only to the progenitor;
likewise when a celibate student (brahmacārī) sits near him or dwells in his proximity.
Yama said: "Indeed, there is no fault for kings, nor for those observing vows, nor likewise for those performing sacrificial sessions;
for they are always seated in the station of Indra and possess the very form of Brahman."
For kings, immediate purification is prescribed in matters of urgent necessity;
for the sake of protecting the subjects, destruction [of enemies] is the cause in such cases.
There is immediate purification for kings due to the obstruction of their duties, and for a Brāhmaṇa for the sake of not interrupting his Vedic recitation.

There is no impurity for kings during royal duties; none for those observing a vow while in the vow; none for those engaged in a sacrificial session (*sattra*) while in that session; none for artisans during their craft; and none for those carrying out the king’s orders by his command. Vṛddha-Parāśara states: "For kings there is no birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), nor for those observing a vow, nor for those engaged in a sacrificial session."
And for all those who have been initiated, the king may choose whomsoever he wishes.
When those who have been initiated, consecrated, or devoted to vows and sacred fords,
as well as those intent on austerity and charity, there is no impurity regarding death or birth.
Śātātapa says: "If kings do not wish to touch someone at their own will, impurity (āśauca) lasts for that very moment of contact. Hārīta says:
A Kṣatriya standing in battle, a Vaiśya in the midst of cattle,
a Brāhmaṇa who is a perpetual sacrificer, and one who is always a celibate student— these are indeed pure.
Jābāla says:
Among a religious student, a king, an ascetic, one who has taken a vow, and one who is consecrated for a sacrifice;
and during a sacrifice, a marriage, or the use of weapons—there is never any impurity (sūtaka).
[64] Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* states:
"A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) should never himself abandon his ritual duties during a period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*),
nor one who has been initiated for a sacrifice after the initiation ceremony, nor one who is performing austerities such as the *kṛcchra* penance."
Even when their father has died, no fault whatsoever attaches to them;
however, at the conclusion of the ritual act, there shall be impurity for three days for those who are religious students (brahmacārin).
“In some cases”: in certain instances, the action [is performed by others].
[Pracetāḥ: Artisans, craftsmen, physicians, as well as female and male slaves.
Kings and the royal servants are declared to be immediately pure.
Yājñavalkya [3.28–29]:

For officiating priests and those initiated for a sacrifice while engaged in sacrificial rites, as well as for those observing the sattra-vow, celibate students, donors, and knowers of Brahman; likewise—
Immediate purification is ordained in cases of giving a gift, at a wedding, during a sacrifice, in battle, during a national calamity,
and even in times of dire distress.
Aṅgiras says: "In birth and in death, impurity does not exist in three cases:
during a sacrifice, at the time of a wedding, and likewise during a Vedic ritual."

[65] Under the continued application of the term "impurity" (*aśauca*), Viṣṇu states (22.53–55): "There is no impurity during the consecration of a deity or at a marriage, provided the preparations have already been made; nor when there is a disturbance of the country; nor even in times of dire distress."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*:
"If an impurity (sūtaka) should occur between a wedding and a sacrifice,
one should have others provide the remaining food and must not touch those eating in the house."
Parāśara states: In times of famine, during the invasion of a kingdom, upon the outbreak of calamities,
and even in the event of death by portents, immediate purification is ordained.
Yama said: "This is the rule for times of well-being, but it is recorded otherwise in times of distress;
when a divine fear has arisen or a primary limb has been destroyed."
Or rather, impurity is said to apply to that matter which was previously intended;
Dakṣa states:
"But all this impurity is proclaimed to apply only during one's own time [of life]."
For everyone who has fallen into calamity, there is no impurity even during a period of birth-impurity.
Now, the definition of sapinda and so forth.
Regarding this, Manu [5.60] states:
"Sapiṇḍa-relationship ceases with the seventh person;
the status of Samānodaka (distant kinsmen) ceases when the birth or the name is no longer known."
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"Sapiṇḍatā for all [relatives] extends to seven generations on the basis of lineage;
the offering of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) and the offering of water, as well as purity and impurity, follow that [sapiṇḍatā]."
Gautama [14.12]: The cessation of receiving almsfood occurs at the seventh or the fifth generation.
Vasiṣṭha [4.17–18]:
Sapiṇḍatva is understood to extend to seven generations; for unmarried women, it extends to three generations.

As stated in the Matsya Purāṇa: "The fourth and subsequent ancestors are the partakers of the *lepa* (smeared drops), while the ancestors beginning with the father are the partakers of the *piṇḍas* (funeral cakes)."
The offerer of the funeral cake (piṇḍa) is the seventh among them; their sapinda relationship extends through seven generations.

[67] Sumantu says: Among Brāhmaṇas who share a single *piṇḍa* and offer the *svadhā* libation, there is a cessation of the religious duty (*dharma*) up to the tenth generation; a cessation of the lineage (*gotra*) occurs at the seventh generation; and a cessation of the *svadhā* offering occurs at the third generation. Otherwise, by the interruption of the *piṇḍa*, purification rites, and other ceremonies, one becomes equal to a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa (*brahmaghn*).
Thus it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
For all social classes (varṇas), the sapta-pauruṣī [sapinda relationship] is to be understood;
beyond that, however, follows the status of being samānodaka (distant kinsmen).
Then, by the power of time, when the names of their births are forgotten there,
even that designation of "samānodaka" (distant kinsmen) perishes on account of that alone.
The self is the father; the father of that [self] is the great-grandfather of the self.
And whoever is the father of even him is likewise the grandfather.
Whosoever is the great-grandfather of the one known as the great-grandfather—
counting upwards from him— he is the primordial great-grandfather of them all.
The grandfather is the second, while the father is the third;
with a uterine brother, one becomes the fourth, even as one's own self.
Likewise, the son of a woman of the same caste is proclaimed as the fifth;
the grandson is the sixth, and the great-grandson is proclaimed as the seventh.
Thus, among these who have died, the living great-grandson [inherits];
these are proclaimed to be the sapinda relations whose wealth is undivided.
[68] Or rather, those uterine brothers who have divided their property with others,
as well as kinsmen (sakulya) who have divided their property, are the partakers of the "lepa" (the smearings) in the Śrāddha and other rites.
For those born of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, the period of sapinda relationship extends to three generations;
this applies even to those born of Brāhmaṇas who share undivided property.
But regarding those who have been divided, there is doubt as to whether they belong to the mother’s lineage;
however, for a maiden of the same caste, the sapinda relationship extends through three generations.
Now, the removal of the deceased.
