Regarding this, Manu [5.92] states:
"One should carry out a dead Śūdra through the southern gate of the city;
but those of the twice-born castes should be carried out through the western, northern, or eastern gates, as appropriate."
Hārīta: One should not carry a deceased person facing toward a village. Manu [5.108]:
While his own kinsmen are present, he must not have a deceased Brahmin carried by a Śūdra;
for that oblation, defiled by the touch of a Śūdra, would not lead to heaven.
Yama said: A Śūdra must not follow after a patron who has become deceased;
because of contact with a Śūdra, those twice-born ones would quickly cease to be destined for heaven.
But that Śūdra who brings the fire, as well as the grass, wood, and sacrificial offerings—
thinking "this is indeed dharma"— is defiled by unrighteousness.

[70] Viṣṇu [19.1–5]: One should not cause a deceased twice-born man to be carried by a Śūdra, nor a Śūdra by a twice-born man. Sons should carry their father and mother; Śūdras should not carry a twice-born father or mother. Those Brāhmaṇas who carry a Brāhmaṇa who is without a protector partake of the heavenly world.
Parāśara [3.41]:
Those twice-born who carry the deceased Brahmin who is without a protector obtain,
step by step, the fruit of a sacrifice in due order.
Yājñavalkya [3.26]:
A Brāhmaṇa must not follow a Śūdra under any circumstances.
Having followed him, he becomes pure by bathing in water, touching fire, and consuming clarified butter.
Now, the funeral rites for a deceased person.
Regarding this, Parāśara (3.15) states:
"For those children who have not yet cut their teeth and for those who have just emerged from the womb,
there is no cremation with fire, no period of impurity, and no water-libation ceremony."
Yama said:
One should bury children in a pit; in this way, Dharma is not violated, while singing the Yama-gāthā and recollecting the Yama-sūkta.

For him there is no cremation with fire, no ritual procedure, and no water libation. Sumantu says: For one under two years of age who has been buried, no water libation should be performed; there is immediate purification.
Hārīta:

Since the consecration with fire (agnisaṃskāra) is performed annually due to the authority of the sacred fires, they do not perform the water-libation rites after that time; some say this applies from the second year onwards. Manu [5.68–80]:
Relatives should place a deceased child who has not yet reached two years of age outside [the village],
having adorned it, upon pure ground, except for the collection of bones.
[72] No funeral rite with fire should be performed for him, nor should the water-libation rite be performed;
having abandoned him in the forest like a piece of wood, they should simply leave him there for three days.
The water-rite should not be performed for one who has not reached three years of age;
however, it may be performed by relatives once his teeth have appeared, or even when his name has been given.
Yājñavalkya [3.1–2]:
One should bury a child less than two years of age and should not offer water for them thereafter;
others, surrounded by their kinsmen, should follow [the corpse] as far as the cremation ground.
He should be cremated with a common fire while those chanting the *Yamasūkta* and the relevant verses do so,
provided he was initiated, according to the ritual procedure for one who maintained the sacred fires, as if he were still alive.
“Upetaḥ” means one who has been initiated (*upanīta*). “Āhitāgnyāvṛtā” means by the procedure of one who has established the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*).
Pāraskara [3.10.5–12] continues with the phrase “if the deceased is less than two years old.”

They bury the body without burning it. If death occurs during a period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), the impurity lasts until the rising [of the sun], just like the birth-impurity; in this case, there is no water-libation rite (*udakakarma*). From the age of two years onwards, all should follow the deceased as far as the cremation ground. According to some, they should do so while singing the *Yamagāthā* and muttering the *Tamasūkta*. If the deceased was one who maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), the procedure from the selection of the burial site onwards is the same up to the departure to the water's edge. They burn him with the domestic fire (*śālāgni*) if he maintained the fires; otherwise, they burn him silently with the village fire.

[73] Regarding the phrase “*antaḥsūtaka*,” the meaning is that if a child dies during the period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*), then the impurity remains for the duration of that *sūtaka*, until its conclusion. Regarding “*dvivarṣa*,” the word “*prete*” (when deceased) is to be supplied. “*Sarve*” refers to all *sapiṇḍas*. “*Itaram*” refers to one who has not yet established the domestic fire (*akṛtāvasathya*).
Vasiṣṭha [4.9–10]: “The water-libation and purification [are required] from two years of age onwards; some say [until] the eruption of teeth.”
The offering of water is performed by the sapinda relatives for one who has grown matted hair, as well as for their women; some say it is for those who have been given away in marriage.
Yama:
If a Brahmin who has maintained the sacred fires is burned by a common fire,
he falls from his status as a Brahmin and is reborn from the womb of a Śūdra.

Vasiṣṭha [4.37]: "If one who has maintained the sacred fires dies while away from home, Gautama says that after performing the cremation rites again, the purification is to be carried out as in the case of a corpse.
Kātyāyana [Śrautasūtra 25.8.8–14]: [The relevant rules follow].

If he should die while away from home, [the performer], wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), having milked a cow that has recently calved (*nivānyā*), should place the vessel on the fire to the south; this applies to both the placing on the fire and the removal. From that very spot, carrying [the remains], holding a fuel-stick underneath, and having arranged *kuśa* grass with its tips pointing north and then turning them so the tips point south, he should scatter it once, as in the rite for the ancestors (*pitṛvat*). Having brought the bodies [of the deceased], setting aside the procedure for a male body, covering them with woolen cloth (*ūrṇābhiḥ*), and sprinkling them with clarified butter (*ājya*), the cremation is performed as before.
"As in the rite for the ancestors" means like the ancestral rites (*paitṛka-karma*). "Scattering" means removing [the vessel]. [This is stated] in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
When one who has maintained the sacred fires dies while staying in a foreign land,
his corpse must not be cremated even with his own fires until [they have been brought to him].
Then, having strewn the altar with kuśa grass from the southern fire,
the knower of the ritual procedures, holding a fuel-stick face-downward, [proceeds].
One should cause that cow in his house, which has been milked by another's calf,
to perform the Agnihotra sacrifice with her own cow’s milk in the same manner.
Afterwards, having consigned the sacred fires into himself, he likewise [consigned] those sacrificial implements.
Indeed, having formed the intention, he should take hold of the very stone;
then, having churned it and performed the bringing forth of the fire, he should burn that corpse.
Yajñapārśva says:
When the sacrificer has died and the funeral pyre has been prepared,
even if the fire is obstructed by rain, how can there be an alternative procedure for the deceased?
Having burned the remainder, one should perform churning among those that have not been burned;
having brought other pieces of wood, one should perform the consecration there.
[75] But when the master has gone abroad, or is dead, or when the destruction of his bones is imminent,
tell me, O knower of sacrifice, the procedure for the distribution of the stalks of the *palāśa* tree.
One should place fifty on the head, ten indeed on the neck,
one hundred on the two arms, and likewise ten on the fingers.
One should strike twenty times on the chest, thirty times on the belly and stomach,
four times on the penis, and six times on the testicles.
One should give a hundred [cows] for the thighs; this is the ritual procedure for the deceased. Furthermore, if the bones should ever be recovered again, [the same rite is to be performed].
In the absence of that [wood], if *palāśa* is available, there is indeed a re-performance;
for the Vājasaneyins, the Śruti prescribes a second [offering] with *yajñavārśva* wood.
Kauśika also states the injunction in other Vedic texts:
"Having burned [the fire], [one should act] upon those very embers that have not been burned. This is the meaning according to the Āśvalāyanagṛhyapariśiṣṭakārikā.
[76] In the absence of bones, having made a substitute with palāśa stalks— one should apply forty on the head, ten on the neck,
thirty on the chest, and likewise twenty on the abdomen.
One should give a hundred [cows] for the two arms, ten for the fingers,
six for the two testicles, and four for the penis alone.
One should give a hundred [coins] for the two thighs, thirty for the knees and shanks, and ten for the toes of the feet; this is the prescribed allotment for the deceased.
Having wrapped it with a woolen thread, one should smear it with barley flour;
having consecrated it according to the rite, one should then take it out from the fires.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "Of the two spouses who have maintained the sacred fires, whichever one dies first on earth,
his body must be cremated by the sapindas using the three sacred fires."
Afterwards, his body, having been smeared with clay, should be cremated with the common (laukika) fire;
however, the body of one who has not maintained the sacred fires (anāhitāgni) should be burned by the twice-born using the domestic (gṛhya) fire.
In its absence, even a male image should be fashioned according to the prescribed rite from three hundred, six hundred, or three hundred and sixty leaves of the *palāśa* tree.
It should be wrapped with great care in the skin of a black antelope;
having bound it with woolen thread, it should likewise be plastered over with barley.
They should likewise be cremated with fire using their own ground flour mixed with water, while saying, "May he go to the heavenly world, svāhā! together with his kinsmen.
Having thus burned the leaf-man, one shall remain impure for three nights. Likewise:
if, upon this being done, a man should somehow arrive there under the delusion that someone has died—
Then, having again invoked the purifier (Agni), he should perform the Āyuṣī sacrifice.
Then, when the leaf-man has been burnt and the placement of the vessels has been performed,
if half of that body is found anywhere among the fires on the limbs,
one should rub those burnt pieces of wood together and burn that half.
If the object has been consumed by fire and its remains cannot be found, [the thief shall pay the value].
Likewise: "Even a pauper who has fallen into some misfortune must not be burned;
he should instead be diligently covered with even a fragment of cloth by someone."
Wherever the body may be short, if it is naked, it must be cremated;
however, it should not be burned entirely without remainder; one should leave some small portion remaining from it.
The cremator should circumambulate [the body] seven times while holding seven fuel-sticks;
likewise, seven blows should be dealt with an axe upon the firebrand.
With a concentrated mind, one should mutter, "Obeisance to you, O flesh-eaters";
the flesh-eaters must not be looked upon, and then one should proceed to the river.
Kātyāyana in the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa* [Gobhilasmṛti 3.21–35] states:
"If the householder becomes weak after the evening oblation has been offered,
the morning oblation should be performed in the same manner, provided he recovers."
Having bathed the weak person and clothed him in clean garments and the like,
one should place him on the ground with his head toward the south, lying on his right side.
Having anointed him with ghee and bathed him, he should be dressed in fine garments and wear the sacred thread;
his entire body should be sprinkled with sandalwood paste and adorned with flowers for the sake of purification.
Having cast pieces of gold into its seven openings and having placed a cloth over his mouth, his sons and other relatives should carry him out.
Taking food in an unbaked clay vessel, one person should follow behind the deceased who is preceded by the fire; half of the food he should cast upon the ground along the way.
Having reached half of the cremation ground, sitting facing south,
and bending his left knee, he should slowly perform [the rite] with sesame seeds, as in the offering of the funeral cakes (piṇḍa).
Then, having bathed with his sons and others, he should construct a large pyre of wood on a pure and suitable plot of ground, characterized by the features of a *caitya* and so forth.
There, having laid him down supine with his head toward the south,
one should place a sruk ladle filled with clarified butter in his mouth and set down a sruva ladle with its tip pointing southward.
The lower fire-drill (araṇī) is placed at the feet facing east, the other [upper drill] on the chest;
the winnowing basket and the wooden cup are on the left and right sides respectively.
Together with the pestle, he placed the mortar face down between his thighs;
there, with eyes free of tears, he remained motionless.
Having performed this with the sacred thread over the right shoulder, remaining silent and facing the direction of the ancestors,
he should then slowly offer it to the fire from the south, with his left knee bent.
"From this you were born; from you may he be born again," thus saying the Yajus mantra, "This one for the heavenly world, Svāhā!"
In this way, the householder is consumed and crosses over all evil deeds;
and he who should cremate him also attains blameless progeny.
Just as a traveler bearing weapons passes through even vast forests without fear,
transcending his own unfavorable state and attaining his desired goal.
Thus, this man, possessed of fire and adorned with sacrificial vessels and weapons,
transcends other worlds and attains the Supreme Brahman itself.
Likewise [3.46–53]:
"In this very same way, the placement of the vessels and so forth should be performed for the one who has maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni).
However, regarding the black antelope skin and other such items, there is a specific distinction prescribed by the Adhvaryu priest."

In the case of death abroad, having brought back the bones and sprinkled them with water from a human [source], one should cremate them after covering them with wool; the placement of the vessels and so forth is as before.
In the absence of bones, one should burn leaves or stalks according to the prescribed procedure, numbering as many as the bones; from that point forward, the period of impurity (sūtaka) begins.
If one who is burdened with a mortal sin (mahāpātaka) should happen by fate to maintain the sacred fires,
his son or another relative shall maintain those fires, for it is proper that this be done until the destruction of the sin.
[80] Then one should perform the penance; or if he dies while performing it, another person should extinguish the domestic fire along with the Śrauta fires and the ritual implements.
One should place both [the fires] in the waters, since fire originated from the waters.
One should give the vessels to a Brahmin, or burn them, or cast them into water.
A woman who remains steadfast [in her resolve] should be cremated according to this very procedure;
it is the established rule that the mantra for offering the fire is not to be employed for her.
One should burn the wife with fire itself, provided she is independent and has not fallen from her status; otherwise, one should have her vessels burned separately nearby.

“*Durbalaḥ*” (the weak) refers to one whose life is not expected to last until the morning *homa* and the giving of gifts. In the phrase “having bathed the weak one,” “*durbalaḥ*” means one whose vital breaths have departed. “*Rātrau vilīnau*” (melted at night) refers to two ladles made of *khadira* wood for the purpose of the *maṇḍala*.
Now, regarding the offering of water,
Baijavāpa says:

Now follows the rite for the deceased (*pretakarma*). Having placed the deceased in the forest and having kindled the fire as prescribed, they return without looking back, wearing single garments and observing vows, led by the youngest. Singing the *Yamagāthā* and muttering the *Yamasūkta*, they lead away day after day [the sacrificial items]: a cow, a horse, a man, and cattle, with the verse: "He by whom he is not satisfied, like a fool with wine... Having gone to the water's edge, they emerge from the water once; then, with the little finger of their left hand, they draw a line in the water, saying, "The smallest is evil. Into that [line], they should offer a single handful of water to the deceased, saying, "Svadhā to such-and-such!"

"With the left hand," [meaning] with the fist in the form of a comb; "he scrapes away" [meaning] "the sin is scraped away"—thus Viṣṇu [19.6–8]. Having carried out the deceased relative and having honored him, they should approach the funeral pyre by the right and perform an immersion in water while still wearing their clothes. Having offered the libation of water for the deceased, they should offer a single rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) upon *kuśa* grass.

Vasiṣṭha [4.11–13]: Having consigned the body to the fire, they enter the water without looking back. They should perform the water-rite with both hands, the left and the right. On odd-numbered days, they face south. [82] Hārīta:
Having carried out [and emerged], having purified the water, and having gone there and bathed, he pours out a handful of water, saying, "May he be satisfied.
Thus say Śaṅkha and Likhita.

Now follows the water-rite (*udakakriyā*). Having descended into the water and then emerged, the relatives of the deceased should not rub their bodies; they should sprinkle water once, facing south-east for a Brāhmaṇa, and facing north or east for a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya. Likewise, having placed their lower garments and sacred threads over their right shoulders (*apasavya*), and having said, "Water from me for the sake of the garment," they should emerge from that water, discard the clothes touched by the deceased, and put on other garments.
Thus it is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
First, having covered [the body] with a cloth, and then being covered by that very same one,
they should perform a bath with fine garments that removes all impurities.
Then, on a stone surface, all the water with sesame seeds should be offered;
ten handfuls (añjali) should be given to each brahmin.
Twelve should be given to a king, fifteen to a Vaiśya,
and thirty should be given to a Śūdra who has gone to the land of the deceased.
Having placed the sacred thread over the right shoulder with the garments,
the Brahmins, facing the southern direction, should offer three handfuls of water to him.
By means of the flow from the left thumb, [the water] may fall upon the ground at some point;
reciting this, one should say: "May the deceased named so-and-so, of such-and-such a lineage, be satisfied by this."

Āśvalāyana [4.4.9–11]: They proceed turning to the left, not looking back. Upon reaching a place where water flows down, they emerge once, offer one handful of water, uttering the name of the deceased's *gotra*, and having emerged, put on other garments. Having wrung these out once, they discard them with their fringes pointing north and sit until the appearance of the stars; or, while the lunar orb is visible, they may enter [the village]. "Turning to the left" (*savyāhvṛtāḥ*) means those whose turnings (*āvṛti*) are to the left.
The procedure for bathing according to Paiṭhīnasi:
Meditating mentally on the deceased, one facing south should offer three handfuls of water. One should cease this from the eleventh day after the death.
Baudhāyana [1.11.22]:

In the event of a death, however, having placed the children in front according to their age, having arranged the sacred threads over the right shoulders (apasavya), having descended to a bathing place, and having immersed themselves once [or thrice], having emerged and sipped water, they should pour out water for him; then, having emerged from there, they sit down [or remain seated].
Pāraskara [3.10.13–21]:

If they should request water for sexual intercourse or for ritual purification, saying, "We shall perform the water-rite," he should say, "Do so, but not again" if the deceased was less than a hundred years old; otherwise, he should simply say, "Do so. All the kinsmen descend into the water as far as the seventh or tenth generation. Or, if they live in the same village, as long as they can remember their relationship. Wearing a single garment with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītin*), they wipe away the water with the ring finger of the left hand, reciting, "Driving away the burning sin. Facing south, they immerse themselves. They pour water once for the deceased from their joined palms, saying, "O [Name], this water is for you."
"Connected" means related by kinship; "sexual intercourse" means a brother-in-law.
Āpastamba [2.15.2–10].

For those related by blood on the mother’s side up to the seventh generation from the father, or for as long as the relationship is known—if they have died, the touching of water (libation) is performed, excluding those who were in the womb and those who died before one year had passed. Among these, the same applies to the mother and father alone, as well as to those who steal [the property]. When a wife or a supreme guru has passed away, one should refrain from eating at improper times. They should assume the appearance of the afflicted: having disheveled their hair, covered themselves with dust, wearing a single garment, facing south, they immerse themselves once and then emerge and sit down. This is done three times. Having poured out water for that purpose, they return to the village without looking back and do what women say. Others teach this very same thing regarding the rest [of the deceased].

[85] Yājñavalkya [3.3–5]: On the seventh or even the tenth day, the kinsmen, facing the direction of the ancestors, enter the water with the mantra: "May the evil depart from us, burning away our sin."
In this manner, the water-rite is performed for maternal grandfathers, teachers, and deceased ancestors;
however, the offering of water out of affection is for friends, married daughters, sisters' sons, fathers-in-law, and officiating priests.
Restraining their speech, they should pour out water once, pronouncing the name and the lineage;
however, students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārins) and those who have fallen from their status (patitas) should not perform the water libation.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"The water-rite (udakakriyā) may be performed at will for one's father-in-law, maternal uncle, pupil, fellow student, and king.
Baudhāyana [1.11.1–7] states:

With reference to birth and death, they declare that for sapindas there is impurity lasting ten days, excluding officiating priests, those initiated for sacrifice, and celibate students. Sapinda-relationship, however, extends to the seventh degree among sapindas. Until the completion of the seventh month, or until the eruption of teeth, the touching of water [for purification] is prescribed. For one who has died before reaching three years of age, the offering of funeral cakes and the rite of water-libation are not ordained;
nor should cremation be performed for such a child until the eruption of teeth.
Some indeed perform [the rite] for maidens who have not been given away in marriage, and some for those already given;
for it is for the sake of winning over the world that women are considered to be without mantras.

[86] Pāraskara [3.10.39–43]: "And likewise for the teacher; and for the two maternal grandfathers; and for unmarried women; for married women, others should perform [the rites], and they [should perform them] for those [others].

'Likewise' means that the procedure beginning with wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (prācīnāvīti) and so forth, as well as the bathing and water-rites for the deceased, are extended [to these cases]. 'For the two maternal grandfathers' means this is extended to the maternal grandfathers and their wives."
Now, those unworthy of water:

Regarding this, Manu [5.89–90] states: "The water-libation rite shall be withheld for those born of vain or mixed unions, for those who persist in the life of wandering mendicants, and for those who commit suicide."
And for women who have resorted to heretical sects, those who act according to their lust,
those who harm the fetus or their husband, and those who drink liquor.

“Of those who abandon themselves,” meaning those who abandon their bodies by their own will rather than according to scriptural injunction; for in the case of a scripturally ordained abandonment of the body, it is said:
“But he who, being old, having lost the capacity for purification rites, and having rejected medical treatment, should kill himself by means of Bhṛgu (a precipice), fire, fasting, or water.”

In that case, because of the statement, "Impurity shall last for three nights and the water-libation rite must be performed," the performance of the water-libation and other rites certainly takes place. —
Yama.
The water-libation rite shall be withheld for those born of vain intermixture, those who have passed away while residing in a different stage of life (āśrama),
and for daughters who have been given away in marriage.
"Those separated from their stages of life" refers to those who have renounced the world (*pravrajita*).
Yājñavalkya [3.6] states:
"Heretics, those who have no refuge, thieves, women who kill their husbands, and those who go according to their own lust, and so forth."
Women who drink liquor, those who commit suicide, and those who destroy their offspring do not partake in the impurity rites or the water libations.

Viṣṇu [22.56–58]: Those who commit suicide and outcasts do not share in the period of impurity (*āśauca*). On the anniversary of the death of an outcast, one should cast away a jar of water with the foot. "One should cast away the jar" means that one should push the jar away with the foot, thinking of it as the deceased; by this, he (the deceased) becomes excluded.
Hārīta states:
For ascetics, for those who have been cast out, for women living according to their own will,
and for daughters who have been given away in marriage, the water-rites may be revoked.
“Outcasts” (*apaviddhāḥ*) means those who have been excluded from their kin. Gautama [20.15–16] states:
“But he for whom the penance ends with death shall become pure upon dying; they should perform all the funeral rites, such as the water libations and so forth.”

[89] Bṛhaspati [Prāyaścitta 84]: "He who indeed causes his own death by means of poison, hanging, or a weapon, must be smeared with impure matter as a corpse; he does not deserve any other funeral rite."

Parāśara [4.4–5]: Those Brahmins who touch a cow that has been killed, as well as one that has hanged itself or been caused to be killed by a Brahmin, as well as those who carry it away and those who burn it with fire— [The following verse from Parāśara 4.6 completes the context: ...all these must perform the penance prescribed for killing a cow, and they shall remain excluded from the company of the twice-born for three months. One who does not perform the penance shall fall into hell. Therefore, one should always avoid such persons. If a Brahmin eats the food of those who have touched a dead cow, he becomes pure by performing the Kṛcchra penance for three days. If he eats the food of those who have carried it away, he is purified by a Kṛcchra; if he eats the food of those who have burned it, he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a Śūdra, he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a Vaiśya, he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a Kṣatriya, he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a Brāhmaṇa, he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a woman, he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a child, he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person of mixed caste (saṅkara), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person of outcaste birth (patita), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a mortal sin (mahāpātakin), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a minor sin (upapātakin), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a grievous sin (guru-pātakin), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a secondary grievous sin (laghu-guru-pātakin), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a light sin (laghu-pātakin), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a very light sin (ati-laghu-pātakin), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of transgression (vyatikramin), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of negligence (pramādika), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of omission (anācarin), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of commission (ācarin), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of association (sahacara), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of inheritance (dāyāda), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of debt (ṛṇin), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of witness (sākṣin), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of perjury (kūṭasākṣin), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of theft (stena), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of adultery (parastrī-gāmī), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of incest (gurutalpaga), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of violence (hiṃsaka), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of cruelty (nṛśaṃsa), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of treachery (drohin), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of betrayal (viśvāsaghātaka), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of ingratitude (kṛtaghna), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of ungratefulness (akṛtajña), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of falsehood (anṛtavādin), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of deceit (māyāvī), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of fraud (vañcaka), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of hypocrisy (dambhin), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of pride (abhimānin), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of arrogance (stabdha), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of vanity (mānī), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of self-conceit (ahaṅkārin), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of egoism (ahaṃkārin), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of attachment (sakta), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of aversion (virakta), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of distraction (vikṣipta), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of confusion (mūḍha), he is purified by a Kṛcchra. If he eats the food of those who have cremated a person who has committed a sin of delusion (bhrānta), he is purified by a Tapta-Kṛcchra.
And those others who follow them, as well as those others who break snares—all of them are joined with sin; I shall declare the atonement for them.

Yājñavalkya [3.5–6]: Students of sacred knowledge (brahmacārins), as well as those who have fallen from their status (patitas), heretics (pākhaṇḍins), those who have no refuge (anāśritas), thieves, women who kill their husbands, and those who follow their lusts, shall not offer water libations.

[Vṛddha-Manu]: Eunuchs and the like, thieves, those who have not undergone the initiatory rites (*vrātya*), those who act contrary to the law, those who harm the fetus or their husband, and women who drink liquor shall not offer water libations.
Manu [5.88, 91]: One who has been initiated for a vow shall not offer water libations until the completion of that vow.
But once it is completed, having offered the water libations, he becomes pure after three nights alone.
Having carried out the funeral rites for one's own teacher, preceptor, father, mother, or guru who has passed away, one who observes a vow is not deprived of that vow.
"Ādiṣṭī" means one who possesses an enjoined vow (*vrata*). Yājñavalkya [3.15] states:
"Even after carrying out the funeral rites for his teacher, father, or preceptor, one who is under a vow remains a *vratī*."
One should not eat food from a cart, nor should one dwell together with such people.
“Sakaṭānna” means food belonging to one in a state of impurity. Vasiṣṭha [23.5]:
For a religious student (brahmacārin) performing funeral rites for anyone other than his mother or father, there is a suspension of his vows until the end of the period.
Baudhāyana [2.1.24]:
For a student, the renewal of the vow occurs through the rite of pacification (śamakarma), except in the case of his mother, father, and teacher.
Now, regarding the removal of grief, Yājñavalkya says [3.7–11]:
When they have finished the water libations, emerged from the water, and are standing upon soft grassy ground after their bath,
one should address them with ancient historical narratives.
He who seeks a core in human existence— which is as pithless as the trunk of a plantain tree and resembles a bubble on the water— is utterly deluded.
If this body, which was composed of five elements, has returned to the state of the five,
what cause for lamentation is there in that, given that it arose from one's own actions?
The earth, which supports all beings, shall perish, as will the oceans and the gods;
how then will the world of mortals, which is like foam, not go to destruction?
Since the deceased helplessly consumes the phlegm and tears shed by his kinsmen, one should certainly not weep; rather, funeral rites should be performed according to one's ability.
Bṛhaspati [Āśaucakāṇḍa 14–18]: Having sat down in a clean place, the kinsmen should console them that day with ancient narratives and old historical legends.
[92] Kings such as Nahuṣa and others, as well as sages whose wealth is their asceticism, have passed under the power of time in this mortal world; what then can be said of one who is like a bubble?
Lamentations and the shedding of tears are of no benefit to one who has died;
having understood this, a wise person should abandon dejection.
Lamentation is never praiseworthy in times of grief;
even ritual action provides no assistance, for there is no help to be found in sorrow.
Therefore, water should be offered for the deceased by kinsmen, sapindas, friends, relatives, and blood relations; that act serves as a benefit to him.
In the Rāmāyaṇa: "But the kinsmen and friends, grieving out of affection,
cause one who has gone to heaven to fall back by their shedding of tears, O Rāghava."
For it is heard, O tiger among men, that in ancient times the most righteous King Bhūridyumna went to heaven by virtue of his meritorious deeds.
Furthermore, O Raghava, because of the tears of grief shed by his circle of kinsmen,
he was cast down from heaven once again when his entire merit had been exhausted.
Your father, the lord, consumed by the fire of excessive grief, has gone to heaven;
possessed by wrath, he might curse you. Therefore, arise, O Raghava!
Likewise: When their union is desired, how can their separation be unpleasant? For union arises already gripped by separation.
In the Mahābhārata:
"Why do you grieve, O fool? Why do you grieve for one who is himself pitiable?
For when they grieve for you, they too shall go to that same destination as those who are pitiable."
Having come from not being seen, he has gone again to being seen;
yet he is neither yours nor are you his—why, then, do you grieve?
There is no absolute cohabitation for anyone with anything,
not even with one's own body, let alone with other ordinary people.
Beings are unmanifest in their origin, manifest in their middle state, O Bhārata, and unmanifest again in their dissolution; what cause for lamentation is there in this?
Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too does it attain another body; the wise man is not deluded by this.
Likewise:
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall;
all unions end in separation; and life ends in death.
Just as two pieces of wood might come together in the great ocean and, having met, drift apart again—
such is the meeting of living beings.
[94] Viṣṇu [20.28–51]: Overcome by time, every living being is led to the next world; since a creature is subject to the noose of karma, what cause for lamentation is there in that?
For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain.
Since this matter is unavoidable, there is no help to be found in this world.
Since grieving people do not benefit the deceased here in this world, one should indeed not weep; rather, the funeral rites should be performed according to one's own ability.
For one who departs accompanied by their good and evil deeds,
what need have they for kinsmen, whether those kinsmen grieve or not?
While the relatives remain in a state of impurity, the deceased finds no rest;
yet once that [impurity] has ended, he approaches those very ones who offer the funeral cakes and water.
Until the sapindikarana rite is performed, one who has died remains a preta;
therefore, offer food along with a water-pot to him who has gone to the world of the ancestors.
And having gone to the world of the ancestors, one eats food at the śrāddha that is equal to nectar;
therefore, offer the śrāddha for him who has gone to the world of the ancestors.
Whether in the state of a deity, in a place of torment, in the animal realm,
or likewise among humans, one receives the śrāddha offered by one's own kinsmen.
When a śrāddha is performed, nourishment for both the deceased and the performer of the rite is certain;
therefore, one should always perform the śrāddha, having abandoned useless grief.
Only this much should always be done for a deceased person by his kinsmen;
a man should not increase the grief of the deceased and of himself.
Seeing the world without refuge and kinsmen dying,
O men, always increase righteousness alone for the sake of a companion.
Even when dead, a kinsman is unable to follow a deceased man;
for, with the exception of one's wife, the path to Yama diverges for everyone.
Dharma alone follows one wherever one goes;
indeed, in this worthless world of mortals, practice Dharma without delay.
One should do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's task in the forenoon;
for death does not wait to see whether one's work is finished or unfinished.
Death seizes and departs with one who is attached to fields, shops, and homes, and whose mind is directed elsewhere, just as a she-wolf carries off a lamb.
[96] Time has no one dear to it, nor is there anyone it hates;
when human karma is exhausted, it forcibly carries away the person.
One whose time has not yet come does not die, even if pierced by hundreds of arrows;
but one whose time has arrived does not live, even if merely touched by the tip of a blade of kusha grass.
Neither medicines, nor mantras, nor burnt offerings,
nor even recitations can save a human being who is overtaken by death or even by old age.
For that which is to come is indeed insurmountable, even by hundreds of obstacles;
one is not able to prevent it—what cause for lamentation is there in that?
Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows,
so too does previously committed karma unfailingly find its doer.
Beings are unmanifest in their origin, manifest in their middle state, O Bhārata, and unmanifest again in their end; what cause for lamentation is there in this?
Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too does it attain another body; the wise man is not deluded by this.
Just as a person here takes up a new garment after discarding one previously worn,
so too does the embodied soul take up a body bound by its own karma.
Just as a person, having cast off worn-out garments, takes up others that are new,
so too does the soul, having cast off worn-out bodies.
The embodied soul departs for other new bodies.
Weapons do not cut this, nor does fire burn it;
water does not moisten it, nor does the wind dry it up.
[98] 20. Now, entering the house.
In this regard, Yājñavalkya (3.12–14) states:
"Having heard this, they should go home with the children at their head;
having bitten neem leaves, they should remain restrained at the door of the house."

Having sipped water (ācamana) and having touched fire and other elements, water, cow dung, and white mustard seeds, they should enter while touching these; then, placing their feet slowly upon a stone, they should proceed.

Hārīta: Those who are younger than the eldest return in the order of seniority. Those who have touched a corpse shall not enter the village until the appearance of the stars; if it is at night, until the appearance of the sun, or with the permission of Brāhmaṇas. With iron vessels in their hands, sleeping on the ground, sitting on the ground, and having cast out a single rice-ball and a handful of water, they shall eat from iron vessels, earthenware, or leaf-cups held in their hands.
Āśvalāyana [4.4.1–17].

They shall remain seated until the appearance of the stars, or they may enter once the orb of the sun is visible. Entering the house with the youngest first and the eldest last, they touch a stone, fire, cow dung, unbroken grains of rice, oil, beans, and water. They shall not cook food on that night; instead, they should subsist on what is purchased or already available. For three nights they should eat food free from pungent condiments and salt, or for twelve nights in the case of the death of a *mahāguru*.
(Pāraskara Gṛhyasūtra 3.10.23–28).

Without looking back, they enter the village in a single file, with the youngest in front. At the door of the house, having bitten off a leaf from a *piṣumanda* tree, and having sipped water for purification, they touch fire, cow-dung, white mustard seeds, and oil; then, having stepped upon a stone, they enter. For three nights, they remain celibate, sleeping on the ground, performing no ritual action nor causing it to be performed. Having purchased or obtained food during the day, they eat it without meat. Having offered a rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) to the deceased, they pronounce his name during the washing, the offering, and the subsequent washing. On that night, they place an earthen vessel containing milk and water in the open air, saying: "O deceased one, bathe here."

“They should not perform [them]”—that is, they should not begin them. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: Having emerged [from the water], one should discard the clothes touched by the deceased and put on others; having offered a *piṇḍa* for that deceased at the door of the house, and subsequently touching blades of young *dūrvā* grass, cow dung, fire, water, and a bull, those entering [the house] should sprinkle their heads or limbs with ghee and white mustard seeds. With weapons in hand and observing the prescribed rules regarding time, they should perform the necessary rites for the deceased at both times of day.
[100] On the ground, they may offer a garland, a ball of food, water, or ointments. At that time, there is a suspension of study and the attendance upon members of the same lineage.
Thus says Baijavāpa.

They touch a *śamī* tree, thinking, "May the *śamī* pacify evil. They touch a stone, thinking, "May I become as firm as a stone; may Agni grant us protection. Having purchased or obtained [the Soma], and having reached home while touching a cow and a goat between them, they should eat food that is saltless for one night. And there is a cessation of ritual activity for three nights.
Thus says Baudhāyana. [BŚS 1.11.22–24]

Having touched charcoal and water at the door of the house, they should remain for ten days subsisting on food that is neither pungent nor salty, sitting near the *daṭa* (the funeral pyre). On the eleventh and twelfth days, the *śrāddha* rite is performed. Regarding the remaining rites, one should conform to worldly custom. "Kaṭa" refers to a bed of straw. The alternative "or on the twelfth day" is an option depending on impossibility. "In the remaining rites" refers to the performance of auspicious ceremonies and the like. Vasiṣṭha [4.14–15]:

Having gone home, they should remain on a bed of straw for three days without eating; [if they are] unable [to do so], they should subsist on what is purchased or obtained. Yājñavalkya (3.16–18): Eating what is purchased or obtained, they should sleep separately on the ground.
[101] Food should be given for three days to the deceased according to the ritual procedure of the Piṇḍayajña.
Water should be kept in the open air for one day, and milk in an earthen vessel; so says Aṅgiras.
The deities residing in cremation grounds are proclaimed to be those of corpses.
For whomsoever the purification of the deceased has been prescribed for the purpose of a sacrifice.
If their rites are never successfully accomplished, or if a sacrifice is performed on their behalf for the sake of a deceased person, then they will curse those who perform them here.
Therefore, kinsmen should not indulge in grief; the water-rite (udakakriyā) must be performed.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Celibacy, dwelling on the ground, and abstaining from meat should be observed by those who have gathered [for the rite]."
And having prepared a pit on the ground according to the prescribed rite, one should offer the funeral cake.
Then worship with perfumes and garlands is prescribed, and thereafter the offering of food. Manu [5.73]:
They should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, and they should immerse themselves in water for three days.
And they should not eat meat, nor should they consume their bodily excretions separately.
Bṛhaspati [Āśauca 19]:

They should sleep and sit on the ground, be dejected, remain impure, and be deprived of enjoyments; they should eat food that is neither pungent nor salty, and likewise subsist only on what is obtained as alms or purchased.

Gautama [14.35–40]: All shall sleep on the ground, remain seated, and observe celibacy. They shall not cleanse themselves. They shall not eat meat until the offering (*pradāna*). Water-libations (*udakakriyā*) are performed on the first, third, fifth, seventh, and ninth days, along with the discarding of their clothes. However, for the lowest castes (*antyānām*), this occurs at the end.

[102] “They shall not cleanse themselves” means they shall not wear bright or polished attire. “Until the offering” means until the performance of the *śrāddha*. Regarding “at the end, however, for the lowest castes,” Bhartṛyajña states that this refers to the conclusion of the ninth period of impurity.
Sumantu: Having cremated [the body], that water should be offered outside by the kinsmen of the same lineage (gotra) for the deceased on the first,
third, seventh, and likewise the ninth day.
Bṛhaspati [Āśaucakāṇḍa 20]: On the first day, the third, the fifth, the seventh,
or the ninth day, the simultaneous discarding of nails and body hair is performed in the presence of a Brahmin.
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"Anointing with oil and the massaging of the limbs of kinsmen [benefit the deceased];
by that, as well as by what his own kinsmen eat, the living being is nourished."
In the Mahābhārata: "Offer water for drinking with sesame seeds and a lamp; stay awake!
Rejoice together with your kinsmen; this is difficult to obtain for those who have passed away."

In the *Āśvalāyanagṛhyapariśiṣṭa*: "The new *śrāddha* lasts for ten days; that mixed with barley lasts for six seasons; beyond this, it is called the ancient (*purāṇa*) *śrāddha*. Thus, the *śrāddha* is said to be threefold."
[103] That *śrāddha* at which the Viśvedevas receive no portion, whether in a new vessel or an old one, shall be considered demonic (*āsura*) and base (*vṛṣala*), being devoid of mantras.
One should first cause [the body] to be placed upon a stone in a place devoid of water, lacking incense, and bereft of perfumes and garlands; thereafter, one should perform the Śrāddha rite.
And afterwards, one should offer the funeral ball (piṇḍa) upon that very spot according to the rule;
whether he be of a different lineage or the same lineage, whether it be a woman or a man, [he may do so].
He who offers [the funeral rites] on the first day must complete them for ten days.
As Hārīta says:
"If one who belongs to a different *gotra* or is a non-relative offers the fire to the deceased..."
He should complete the offering of water and the presentation of funeral cakes within ten days.
Following the word "abstention" (*vairamaṇe*), Āpastamba [1.10.4–9] states:

"In the case of the mother, the father, or the teacher, there are twelve days [of impurity]. During those periods, there is contact with water for that duration. And for those who follow [the deceased], there is the shaving of the hair. Some say that those who have returned home from their studies (*samāvṛtta*) should not shave, except at the time of the *vivāra* (the opening of the hair). Furthermore, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: 'He who is shaven is empty and uncovered; this [hair] which has been cut is his covering. In the case of sacrificial sessions (*satra*), there is shaving of the topknot (*śikhā*) because of a specific scriptural injunction. Hārīta says:

They should bathe on the third, fifth, and seventh nights. On the ninth day, they should give away their clothes for the sake of purification. On the tenth day, having gone to the forest, having had their hair and beards shaved, having discarded their soiled garments, having rubbed themselves with a paste of sesame seeds, having bathed their heads with white mustard seeds, and wearing either new or white garments, they should step upon a stone and, after touching a cow, gold, and other such items, re-enter [the village]. Having performed a rite of pacification (*śānti*) and offered the *ekoddiṣṭa* śrāddha on the following day, they resume their religious duties, beginning with rites for well-being (*svastyayana*). Purity of lineage is threefold: through conduct (*ācāra*), through tradition (*āmnāya*), and through ritual action (*kṛtya*). "Conduct" refers to what is established in the world and what is established in the Veda; "tradition" is that which is explained in the world through legal procedure and the like; and "purity through ritual action" refers to the performance of rites.

Viṣṇu [19.18–23]: Having departed from the village at the end of the period of impurity, and having performed the *śvaśru-karman* (the rite for the mother-in-law), they should enter their home after bathing with a paste of sesame or mustard seeds and changing their clothes. There, having performed a propitiatory rite (*śānti*), they should perform the worship of the Brahmins. The gods are the invisible gods; the Brahmins are the visible gods. By the Brahmins the worlds are sustained.
Through the grace of the Brahmins, the deities abide in heaven.
The word spoken by a Brahmin never becomes false at any time.
Whatever the Brahmins say with the greatest satisfaction,
the deities rejoice at that; when they are satisfied, the deities are constantly satisfied.
The gods who are beyond perception [are superior] to the gods who are perceived directly.
Paiṭhīnasi says:

On the following day, having established the sacred fire, one should perform the *śāntyudaka* (water for peace). First, with the hymn beginning *śaṃ no devīḥ*. Second, with two verses: *śaṃ no devīḥ* and *agnaye naḥ*. Third, with the three verses: *śaṃ na indrāgnī*, *tad astu mitrāvaruṇā*, and *śaṃ no dhātā*. Fourth, with the four verses: *indra jīva*, *yasmāt kośāt*, *pṛthivī*, and *śāntiḥ*. In both cases, and everywhere, one should recite the *Sāvitrī*. At the third [rite], having sipped water with the left hand, one should spit out gravel and *kuluttha* (horse-gram). The verse *vivasvān indram* has already been mentioned. On the tenth night, having had his hair, beard, body hair, and nails shaved, he should perform the *śāntyudaka* for the sake of his own peace. He should feed an odd number of Brahmins.

In the passage beginning with "first," the connection is with the phrase "one should prepare the water for pacification. "With two" refers to the two mantras that will be mentioned below. "Having sipped water with the left hand" means having tasted [water] with the left hand.
On this point, there are two verses:
"When, in the rite of birth-impurity (sūtaka), no performer is found after the deceased has passed away..."
Having fasted for ten nights and bathed, he himself should perform the rite of the water of pacification.
[106] He who is capable of performing this rite here, subsisting on air for three nights and bathing on the fourth day, shall thereafter attain peace.
Manu [5.99]: A Brahmin shall become pure by touching water; a Kṣatriya, by his vehicle and weapons;
a Vaiśya, by his goad and reins; and a Śūdra who has performed his duties, by a staff.
Devala says:
When the days of impurity have passed, having bathed well and performed auspicious rites,
they are freed from that impurity after having caused the Brahmins to pronounce blessings.
Now, the collection of the bones.
In that regard, Viṣṇu [19.10–12] states:
"On the fourth day, they should perform the collection of the bones. And these should be cast into the waters of the Gaṅgā.
As long as a human bone remains in the waters of the Gaṅgā..."
For that many thousands of years, he is honored in the heavenly world.
Kātyāyana [Śrautasūtra 25.8.1–8]

On the fourth day, having fed the Brahmins who have not been invited, he turns the bones over with a Palāśa twig, takes them up with his thumb and little finger, and places them in a Palāśa leaf-cup. [He places *śamyākā* wood and mud in the cemetery. Having anointed the bones with fragrant sandalwood and the like and sprinkled them with water, he digs a trench extending toward the south-east, spreads *kuśa* grass within it, and scatters either cloth or turmeric, saying, "O So-and-so, I deposit you here with this mind, with this afflicted speech, with the sacred word, with the threefold knowledge, upon the earth, the imperishable, with the essence of the waters. This is the Vājasaneyaka version; or else [he uses]: "With this mind, with this afflicted speech, with the sacred word, with the threefold knowledge, I deposit you, O So-and-so, upon the earth, the imperishable, with the essence of the waters. For one desiring to construct a cemetery, the collection [of bones] is done in a jar; and the depositing is performed silently.
In the *Chandogapariśiṣṭa*, Kātyāyana [as cited in the *Gobhilasmṛti* 3.54–58] states:
"The collection of the bones may take place on the following day or on the third;
the procedure for that which was prescribed by the sages is now being declared."

Having performed everything up to the ritual bath as before, he should then sprinkle all the bones with cow's milk, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder and reciting the *abhāṣan* mantra.
Having repeatedly removed the ashes with branches of the *śamī* and *palāśa* trees,
and having sprinkled it with clarified butter, one should moisten it with fragrant water mixed with cow's products.
Having placed [the bone] in a pair of earthen vessels, one should wrap them with thread;
then, having bathed at a pit, one should bury them in pure ground while facing south.
Having filled the pit with mud mixed with a lump of earth and aquatic moss,
and having leveled the surface above, one should perform the remaining rites according to the procedure for the forenoon.

This very same rule is declared for one who has died without having maintained the sacred fires; the procedure for women should be the same as that for those without fires. Now, therefore, what has not been mentioned is being stated.

Āśvalāyana Gṛhya Sūtra [4.6.1–8]: The collection of the bones (saṃcayana) takes place after the tenth day of the dark fortnight, under an odd-numbered lunar mansion and a single asterism. A male [is placed] in a jar without markings; a female, in one without markings. [The assistants] should be an odd number, not paired, and advanced in years. Moving three times from right to left around the site, he sprinkles it with milk and water using a branch of the *śamī* tree, reciting: "O cool one, O thou who art possessed of coolness... They should deposit the bones one by one, moistening them with their thumbs and ring fingers, placing the feet first and the head last. Having collected them so as to form a well-arranged whole and having honored them with a fan, [the rite is concluded].
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Having bathed, they perform the water-libation for the deceased for three nights;
thereafter, on the fourth day, they perform the sacrifice to the deity of the cremation ground."
For Śaṅkara and the other deities residing there are worshipped by those who have bathed,
put on well-washed garments, and approached the vicinity of the cremation ground.
With materials prescribed for one's own caste, gathered according to one's ability,
in earthen vessels and in sacrificial ladles (carus) used for the rites.
The flesh-eating deities are to be honored with well-cooked foods and edibles, milk-rice, drinks, as well as fruits and roots grown in the forest.
Some should offer the water of honor (arghya), while others should offer beautiful flowers;
incense, lamps, and garlands should likewise be offered by some with haste.
The vessels were filled all around the cremation fire;
some of them were to be offered, as were all those that had been sprinkled here.
All of them, having adorned themselves, should announce what is to be said:
"Homage always to the gods who have the faces of flesh-eaters."
Whatever eternal and venerable deities may reside in this cremation ground,
may they accept from us this imperishable eight-limbed offering.
May they bestow upon this preta eternal and auspicious worlds;
may they grant us the boon of long life, health, and happiness.
Having thus offered all the bali-oblations and sprinkled them with milk, those who are restrained in speech and composed in mind should perform the dismissal of the deities.
Then, having taken a branch from a sacrificial tree,
one who is a member of the same lineage (*sagotra*), remaining silent, should put on his garment in the *apasavya* manner in the prescribed order.
Having bathed all the bones of the deceased, including those from the principal limbs,
with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and having wrapped them in a linen cloth;
Having placed it in a new earthen vessel that is well-covered and auspicious,
one should establish it in a forest or at the foot of a pure tree.
Then, having slowly carried it from that place to the waters of the Ganges,
either a grandson or a brother shall quickly cast it therein.
Having taken the bones and that ash, one should carry them away and cast them into water;
thereafter, the ground should be swept clean with cow-dung and water.
And worship with flowers, incense, and so forth, as well as with offerings, should be performed in sequence as before.
Furthermore, for the purpose of covering the ground, there should be either a tree or a lotus.
[111] Or a cloth-strip should be struck there by all those together with their kinsmen;
thereafter, they must perform a ritual bath with their clothes on according to the prescribed rule.
Likewise: in some cases, on the third day for a Brahmin, on the fourth for a Kṣatriya,
on the fifth for one of Vaiśya birth, and on the tenth day for a Śūdra.
The collection of bones for one who has died is performed out of respect for the local custom;
this same procedure applies even to living members of the castes when they come into contact [with the corpse].
In the fourth [generation] for Brāhmaṇas, and in the fifth for kings as well;
in the ninth for those of the Vaiśya caste, and beyond the tenth for Śūdras.
Men should perform the śrāddha rite according to the requirements of place and time;
for there are those who share the same funeral cakes (sapiṇḍas), as well as those of the same caste, and others who are hungry.
The poor, the helpless, and the wretched eat even food there;
likewise: "On the second day, during the three-day period of impurity, the collection of bones must be performed."
Regarding immediate purification, it is settled that it must be performed at that very moment.
Likewise: "Those who occasionally carry the bones of their parents and ancestors to the waters of the Gaṅgā,"
For those who are endowed with true being and overcome by compassion,
their sacred fords indeed bestow fruit.
Or, having avoided two families—
the one belonging to his mother and the one belonging to his father’s birthplace—
a Brahmin carrying the bones of another [is purified].
He incurs the exhaustion of his fortune and evil karma.
Then, having reached the bank of the Bhāgīrathī and taking the bones of both families there,
a man, desiring to cast them [into the river] with devotion, [proceeded].
Having beheld the Bhāgīrathī, he attained purity.
Then, having bathed and sprinkled [the image] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and having combined it with flowers, sesame seeds, perfumes, incense, and so forth,
one should place it within a hollowed-out lump of clay.
He beheld the direction crowded with throngs of hungry ghosts.
Having entered the water while reciting "Homage be to the Dharma," he should cast [the flower] with the words "May he be pleased with me.
Then, having risen and gazed upon the radiant sun, he should look at the sun.
One should give it, along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), into the mouth of a Brahmin.
When this has been done, for one dwelling in the city of the departed, there shall be a transition to heaven equal to that of Mahendra.
Likewise:
"Excluding the mother's family and the father's family, that lowest of men who takes bones originating from another family shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance."

Thus ends the section on the Purity of Lineage (*kulaśuddhi*) in the *Kṛtyakalpataru*, composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Mallakṣmīdhara, the son of Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara, who served as the Great Minister for Peace and War (*mahāsāndhivigrahika*) to His Majesty the Emperor (*mahārājādhirāja*), the illustrious Govindacandradeva.
[114] 22 Now, the purification of the body.
In this regard, Manu and Viṣṇu state:
"Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water,
smearing [with cow dung], wind, ritual action, the sun, and time are the agents of purification for embodied beings."
Of all forms of purity, purity in wealth is declared to be the highest;
for he who is pure in wealth is truly pure, not he who is merely purified by earth and water.
The wise are purified by patience; those who have committed forbidden acts by giving;
those whose sins are concealed by silent recitation; and those most learned in the Vedas by austerity.
That which is to be purified is cleansed by earth and water; a river is purified by its current;
a woman defiled in mind is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born is purified by renunciation.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the inner self is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom.

[115] “Knowledge” (*jñāna*) refers to that taught in Sāṃkhya and Yoga, which is internal. “Austerity” (*tapas*) refers to the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, and other such penances. “Food” (*āhāra*) refers to the most pure substances, such as milk and barley-gruel, when they have been prepared. “Mind” (*manas*) is the cause of purification by means of its volitions (*saṃkalpa*). “Smearing” (*upāñjana*) refers to the application of cow-dung and the like. “Ritual action” (*karman*) refers to the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and so forth. “Purity regarding wealth” (*arthaśauca*) consists of avoiding the taking of what has been given improperly and similar acts. Those who are wise are purified “by forbearance,” that is, by knowledge alone; for they are not afflicted by hatred, envy, and malice, which are causes of impurity. “By austerity” means by the study of the Vedas and by the knowledge thereof, as it is said: “For a Brāhmaṇa, austerity is knowledge. However, the *kṛcchra* and other penances are a cause of purification for everyone, not only for those who know the Vedas. By the statement “a river is purified by its current,” it is meant that even in the absence of contact with a vessel or the like, the river becomes pure in another location due to the force of its current, provided it is devoid of the taste and smell [of the impurity]; it is not the case that there is impurity everywhere as in the case of a well. “Corrupted in mind” (*manoduṣṭā*) means possessing merely a longing for another man. “By menstrual flow” (*rajasā*) means by the menses. “By renunciation” (*saṃnyāsena*) means by the undertaking of the fourth stage of life (*āśrama*). “The elemental self” (*bhūtātmā*) is the living soul (*jīva*). “Intellect” (*buddhi*) is corrupted by an adherence to non-existent objects—that is, by the determination of a distinction between the nature of a thing and the form of an object where none exists. Regarding this, Medhātithi says: “It is purified by knowledge,” meaning by the development of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which rests upon self-luminosity.
Yājñavalkya [3.31–34]: Time, fire, ritual action, earth, wind, mind, knowledge, austerity, water,
repentance, and fasting— all these are causes of purification.
[116] For those who have committed forbidden acts, giving gifts and the current of a river bring purification;
for one requiring cleansing, it is clay and water; and for the twice-born, renunciation is indeed the means of purification.
Austerity is said to be the water for those who know the Vedas, patience for the wise, water for the body,
and truth for the mind of those whose sins are concealed by austerity.
For the elemental self (bhūtātman), austerity and knowledge are the means of purification; for the intellect (buddhi), it is wisdom (jñāna);
and for the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), purification through the knowledge of the Lord (īśvara) is considered supreme.
Yama said: Truthfulness is purity, austerity is purity, restraint of the senses is purity,
compassion toward all beings is purity, and the fifth is purity by means of water.
Likewise:
"Vessels are purified by water; the mind by truth or by wisdom;
the elemental self by austerity; the intellect by knowledge; and the wise man by forgiveness."
Bṛhaspati [Āśaucakāṇḍa 52]: The body is purified by earth and water; one who has been possessed by a spirit is purified by exorcism;
an embodied being is purified by learning and austerity; and the intellect is purified by knowledge.
The destruction of sin occurs through the private recitation of scripture, through remorse, through burnt offerings, and through austerity;
likewise, the exhaustion of evil comes about through meditation, residence in sacred places, and through giving.

[117] Likewise, [Āśaucakāṇḍa 54–56]: Not hearing the slander of others and not looking at the wives of others—this is the purification of the ears and the eyes; freedom from backbiting is the purity of the tongue.
Abstaining from killing living beings, refraining from theft, cleanliness of the hands and feet,
and avoiding intimacy with women— this is prescribed as bodily purity.
This entire purification, both external and internal, has been declared in its entirety;
furthermore, the Self-existent One himself proclaimed the purification of wealth to be superior to all.
Vasiṣṭha says: Time, fire, satisfaction of the mind, water, humility,
and that which is unknown to living beings— these sixfold means are held to be purifying.
“Unrecognized” means that the harm inflicted by a wicked person has not been perceived.
Baudhāyana [1.8.2–4]:
The limbs are purified by water; the intellect is purified by knowledge.
And by non-violence toward living beings, the self is purified through the mind and truth.
Purity of mind is internal purity. We shall now explain external purity. Thus it is heard [in the scriptures]: "Purity is said to be twofold, that which is practiced by the cultured (śiṣṭas)."
And by non-violence the inner self is purified, and the mind is purified by truth.
[118] Again, Baudhāyana [1.8.47–48]: Time, fire, purity of mind, smearing with water and the like,
and that which is unknown to living beings— this is said to be the sixfold purification.
Impurity is prescribed after having taken into account the place, the time, as well as oneself, the object, the purpose of the object, the cause, and the state.
Hārīta [A. 19], continuing from the term "purity," states:
"Internal purity is fivefold: mental, visual, olfactory, vocal, and auditory. Hārīta has also explained the nature of these, beginning with the mental, along with their methods of purification.

That which is designated as non-meritorious (*apuṇya*) is a cause of impurity for the mind; that which is designated as meritorious (*puṇya*) purifies. Non-merit consists of malice toward others and the like; merit consists of the contemplation of Viṣṇu and other [deities]. Regarding the visual sense, however, there is impurity upon seeing impure substances and the like; purification occurs from seeing the sun. Even if one intentionally and deliberately sees another’s naked wife, there is no purification by means of the sun. Even when performed for the sake of that [purification], an act possesses the power to cleanse because it is the opposite of what is designated as otherwise. Regarding the olfactory sense, impurity arises from smelling the odor of onions and such; when smelled, one becomes pure through three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*). Regarding the vocal sense, impurity arises from speaking untruth; there is a re-washing of the hands.
[119] Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"For those who sacrifice to the Self, purification of the body is by means of water and earth; for those whose selves are purified, purification of the intellect is by means of knowledge, and purification of the self is by means of austerity.
The meaning is that for those who sacrifice to the Self, the intellect becomes pure through knowledge.

Likewise, there is purification through restraints (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), mantras, vows (*vrata*), fasting (*upavāsa*), and so forth, from defects inherited from one's maternal and paternal lineages. — Uśanas.

Hereafter, we shall explain the chapter on purification (*śaucādhyāya*). In that regard, purification is of two kinds: external and internal. Purification (*śauca*) consists in turning away from those things censured by the intellect and the ego. External purification also concerns the removal of odor, smears, and oily residues; it is held that purity is achieved through the sprinkling of water, which removes odor, color, touch, and oiliness.

“From those blameworthy acts involving intellect and egoism”—here, *buddhi* refers to that which consists of doubt; *ahaṃkāra* is the conceit "I alone am superior"; and *nindita* refers to drinking liquor and similar acts. “By sprinkling with water”—the meaning is that external purity (*bāhya-śauca*) consists in the removal of odors and other such impurities. Again, Uśanas says: therein, purity of heart (*hṛdaya-śauca*) is the goodness of the mind characterized by freedom from malice; purity of action (*karma-śauca*) is the avoidance of censurable deeds; bodily purity (*śārīra-śauca*) is [attained] through earth and water; purity of speech is the avoidance of what is unpleasant, untruthful, or harsh; and there is also the prohibition of false intentions even in the mind.
[120] Paiṭhīnasi:
Having touched semen or urine that has become defiled by food remnants, one becomes pure after wiping the area, sipping water, and washing that spot three times. Viṣṇu [23.42]: [The same].
Then, for all living beings that have been excessively defiled, one should diligently perform purification with earth and water; there is no other means of purification for them.
For the purpose of purification after voiding feces or urine, earth and water should be taken in appropriate quantities;
likewise for the purification of the twelve bodily impurities.
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, sweat,
phlegm, tears, rheum of the eyes, and perspiration— these twelve are the impurities of human beings.
“Dūṣikā” refers to eye-secretion. Devala states: “Impurity arises especially from the entry of food and other such substances.”
One becomes impure by touching those who have fallen [from their caste], as well as the impure and the unclean.
From dreaming, from the changing of clothes, from injury, or from the fatigue of travel;
or after speaking words that are bitter, false, or even cruel.
Having observed the body pierced by perspiration, one should sip water and become pure;
in the case of impurity caused by ointments, oils, or odors, there must be their removal.
They say that the characteristic of purity consists in the removal of smears, moisture,
and odors to a great distance by means of earth, water, cow dung, and so forth.

Afterwards, the rule for sipping water (ācamana) for the sake of purification will be stated. By the phrase "pierced by trickling [saliva]," being pierced by phlegm and so forth is indicated. The words "the rule will be stated" refer to that of sipping water; this is the ellipsis. Thus says Hārīta.

Now, concerning the body: when there is contact with those who are wicked, falsely accused, fallen, animals, or those of lower caste, or when the exterior of the body is defiled by sweat, pus, blood, vomit, spittle, dust, mud, food-remnants, water, feces, urine, excrement, and so forth, one becomes pure from that bodily defilement by means of unblemished earth and water, and by employing ashes, cow dung, medicinal herbs, mantras, and the performance of auspicious rites according to the prescribed rules.

“Corrupt persons” (*duṣṭāḥ*) refers to Caṇḍālas and the like. “A person of lower caste” (*adhovarṇaḥ*) refers to a Śūdra. “One who is afflicted” (*upahataḥ*) refers to one possessed of leprosy or similar diseases. “Mantras” (*mantrāḥ*) refers to the Aghamarṣaṇa and others. “Auspicious conduct” (*maṅgalācāraḥ*) refers to the performance of auspicious rites involving white mustard seeds and the like. In this regard, purity arises through the procedure employed by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), which consists of an optional combination (*vikalpitasamuccaya*) of ashes and other such items. Viṣṇu [22.77–80]:

If one is defiled by bodily impurities below the navel or on the forearms, or by wine and intoxicants, that limb shall be purified by washing it with earth and water. If defiled elsewhere, that limb shall be purified by washing with earth and water followed by a bath. If defiled by the mouth, however, one shall fast, bathe, and purify oneself with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). This also applies to being defiled by the lips; "lips" (*daśanacchada*) here refers to the fangs. Thus says Aṅgiras.
If any part of the body above the navel—excluding the hands—is struck [by an impure substance], one must bathe;
however, that which is below the navel is purified by washing alone.
If, at any time, impurity should enter through a sense organ,
or if it has reached there by touching the mouth, bathing is the means of purification.
Śaṅkha states:
"If a man touches with anything above the navel the mud or water from a street, or saliva and the like, he becomes pure immediately by bathing."
[Yama]: But if one enters a village settlement during the rainy season while covered in mud,
it is prescribed that three applications of clay be used for the shanks and twice as many for the feet.
“Grāmasaṃkaraḥ” means the refuse of a village.
Now, regarding purification through bathing, Manu states (5.85–87):
"A Divākīrti, a woman in her courses, an outcast, and likewise a woman who has recently given birth..."
Having touched a corpse or one who has touched it, one becomes pure by bathing.
Having sipped water and being purified, one should always mutter, upon seeing something impure, solar mantras according to one's enthusiasm and *pāvamānī* verses according to one's ability.
Having touched a human bone that still has fat or marrow on it, a Brahmin becomes pure by bathing;
however, if it is free of fat or marrow, he becomes pure simply by sipping water (ācamana) and then touching a cow or looking at the sun.

“Divākīrti” refers to a *caṇḍāla*. Here, those who have been touched by him—such as the *divākīrtis* and others—are to be understood.
