And this bath, even if immersion in water is impossible, must be performed with hot water as well, because of the statement of Śaṅkha: “Purification of the body is to be known as occurring through that which has been heated by fire. “Upon seeing the impure” means upon seeing the impure, such as *divākīrtis* and others.
In the *Brahmapurāṇa*: “Having touched a human bone, whether it be burnt or even devoid of fat...”
One should bathe, touch a cow, look at the sun, and remember Viṣṇu.
And this bathing after touching a bone devoid of flesh pertains to intentional contact; however, touching a cow or similar animals pertains to unintentional contact. Manu [5.144] states:
"One who has vomited or been purged, having bathed, should perform the consumption of ghee."
One should indeed sip water after eating food; bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse.
[Śātātapa]:
"During the fertile period, bathing is prescribed for one who has engaged in sexual intercourse because of the possibility of conception;
however, outside the fertile period, purification must always be performed as in the case of voiding urine or feces."
Yama states: "In cases of indigestion, at dawn, after vomiting, after shaving, after sexual intercourse,
upon having a bad dream, or after touching a wicked person, only bathing is prescribed."
The term "abhyudite" (when the sun has risen) is intended as an indicator for the time when the meal has been left over. Gautama [14.29–31]:

Upon touching one who has fallen from his caste, a Caṇḍāla, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, a corpse, or one who has touched them—or upon touching someone who has touched such a person—one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on. And the same applies to a dog; some say this applies whenever one is struck by it.

The word *upasparśana* (touching) is connected with each term individually. Therefore, the meaning is that upon touching an outcast (*patita*), a *caṇḍāla*, a woman who has recently given birth (*sūtikā*), a menstruating woman (*udakyā*), or a corpse; or upon touching one who has touched an outcast and so forth; or even upon touching one who has touched the latter, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on. Here, the requirement of bathing with clothes on for the third person who touched the one who touched the object is stated as referring to cases where the act was intentional. However, regarding cases where the act was unintentional:
"If a man touches someone who has touched an impure thing, or even a third person, he becomes pure by washing his hands and feet with water and performing *ācamana*."
Thus it should be understood as stated by Devala. Bṛhaspati [Āśauca 49] states:
"Having intentionally touched an outcaste, a woman who has recently given birth, an outcaste of the lowest class, or a corpse..."
Having performed a bath with one's clothes on and having consumed clarified butter, one becomes purified.
Devala says: A dog-cooker (outcaste), one who has fallen from his caste, one who is deformed, one who is insane, a corpse-bearer,
a woman who has recently given birth, a woman who miscarries, and a woman overwhelmed by her menses.
Having touched domestic dogs, chickens, or pigs,
a person becomes pure by bathing with their clothes on and including the head at that very moment.
If one who is himself impure should touch these [objects] which are also impure,
he becomes purified again by means of the *upavāsa* fast or, alternatively, by the *kṛcchra* penance.
If a person has touched something impure, he becomes pure by sipping water for a third time,
and then washing his hands and feet with water and performing the ritual sipping (ācamana).
"Or again, with difficulty" refers to the subject of repeated practice. Likewise:
human bone, fat, excrement, menstrual blood, urine, and semen.
If one should touch the marrow or even the blood of another person, [one must perform penance].
Having bathed, wiped away the bodily excretions and so forth, and sipped water (ācamana), he becomes pure;
by touching those very same [limbs] of his own and performing the wiping, he shall be purified.
Baudhāyana: In traveling on a road together with a Cāṇḍāla, one must bathe with one's clothes on.
Yājñavalkya [3.30]: [same].

If he is touched by those who are menstruating or impure, he should bathe; if he is touched by them [in turn], he should sip water. He should also mutter verses containing the word "water" and recite the Gāyatrī mantra once mentally.

“Touched by them”: touched by those such as *caṇḍālas* or menstruating women (*udakyā*) who have themselves been touched by a staff or similar object; “touched” means contacted. “He should sip water” (*upaspṛśet*) means he should perform *ācamana*. “The *abliṅga* verses” refers to the three beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*. And thus, the statement of Manu [5.85], “A corpse and one who has touched it,” concerns the case of direct contact. [127] Parāśara [12.25]:
A sacred tree (*caityavṛkṣa*), a funeral pyre (*cit*), a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), a *caṇḍāla*, and a seller of Soma—[these are impure].
But having touched these, a Brāhmaṇa should enter the water with his clothes on.
Likewise [5.6]:
For that which has been licked by dogs or crows, or torn by their claws,
purification is achieved by washing with water and by singeing with fire.
“Upacūḍana” means touching the crest of a flame.
Āpastamba and Baudhāyana [Āp 1.15.16–18; BDh 1.11.37–38]:

One who has been struck by a dog should plunge into water with his clothes on. Alternatively, having washed that spot and touched it with fire, and having washed his feet again and sipped water, he becomes pure.
"Struck by a dog" means touched by a dog. "With one's clothes on" means wearing one's upper garment. Immersion with one's clothes on pertains to contact above the navel. Hārīta states:

Having touched a dog-cooker (śvapaca), a wrestler (muṣṭika), a corpse-bearer (pretahāraka), or a dead body, one becomes pure by bathing within the water while reciting these [mantras] beginning with "O divine waters. This also applies in cases of indigestion, vomiting, shaving, sexual intercourse with a woman of the same womb (sister), or intercourse during the day.

"Muṣṭika" refers to a Mleccha. [128] Viṣṇu [22.66]: Upon inhaling the smoke from a funeral pyre, all social classes (varṇas) should perform a bath; likewise after sexual intercourse, a bad dream, when blood has reached the throat, and after vomiting or purging. Also after shaving, and after touching one who has touched a corpse, or a menstruating woman, a Cāṇḍāla, or a sacrificial post (yūpa). Except for edible items, one should not wear a garment that has been in contact with the corpse of a five-toed animal or its bone while still moist with fat. In all these instances, one should not wear a garment that has not been washed.
Paiṭhīnasi:

In the event of seminal emission or vomiting, one must bathe with one's clothes on and consume clarified butter. Upon being scratched by a crow or having hair pulled out, one must bathe with one's clothes on. For voiding urine or excrement without water available, one must bathe with one's clothes on and perform a *mahāvyāhṛti* oblation. Upon touching a donkey, a camel, or a *caṇḍāla*, one must bathe with one's clothes on.

"In 'skandane'"—the word "of semen" is to be supplied. "In 'kākakeśamalane'" means in the crushing of a crow's hair. "In 'anudakamūtrapurīṣakaraṇe'" means in the delay of purification after voiding urine or feces. Regarding the term "with fat," the *vyāhṛti* oblation applies when the act is intentional; in this very case, the *Mānava* rule regarding bathing with one's clothes on refers to an unintentional occasion. Kāśyapa [states as follows]:

In the case of touching a *caṇḍāla*, a dog-eater (*śvapaca*), a cemetery, a slaughterhouse, a corpse-bearer, or a woman who is menstruating or has recently given birth; or upon sunrise or sunset, or after having ejaculated, or when there is loud wailing, or when someone cries out in one's ear, or upon ascending a funeral pyre, or upon touching a sacrificial post (*yūpa*)—in these cases, there is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Having informed the Brahmins and bathed with one’s clothes on, one should mutter the verse beginning with “*punar manaḥ*” (*Punarmanaḥ punarāyuḥ*, etc., Mādhyandina 1.2.3). One should offer seven oblations with the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*). Thereafter, purification occurs. This refers to an intentional act. [129] Thus, in the *Vāyupurāṇa*.

Having touched a woman in her courses, a woman who has recently given birth, a dog, an outcaste living on the outskirts of the village, those who are naked and so forth, or those who carry the dead, purification is prescribed.
Having bathed with his clothes on, a man shall become pure by means of twelve applications of clay;
this same purification applies likewise after sexual intercourse and after vomiting.

Cyavana says: Having touched a dog, an outcaste (śvapāka), the smoke from a corpse, one who subsists on the property of the gods, a village priest, a sacrificial post, wood from a funeral pyre, liquor, a liquor vessel, a human bone with fat, something touched by a corpse, a woman in her courses, a great sinner (mahāpātakin), or a corpse—one should plunge into water with one's clothes on, emerge, and touch fire. One should mutter the Gāyatrī one hundred and eight times. Having consumed clarified butter and bathed again, one should sip water three times.
This also applies to cases of intentional and habitual practice.
Śātātapa says:
A washerman, a leather-worker, those who live by hunting and bird-catching, a laundryman, an actor, and likewise a fowler; [these are to be avoided].
Likewise, one with a mouth-opening [like a vulva], a dog, a woman who has intercourse with men of all castes,
one who bears the discus or the banner, a killer of those condemned to death, and one who keeps village cocks and pigs;
If any part of the body other than the head of twice-born men should be touched by these,
one attains purity by washing it with water and performing the ritual sipping (ācamana).
In the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa (35.36–8):

"A knower of dharma [should avoid] those whose food is not to be eaten, women who have recently given birth, eunuchs, cats, rats, dogs, and cocks; as well as the outcaste, the discarded, the Cāṇḍāla, and those who carry the dead."
[130] A woman in her courses and a village pig become pure by bathing after touching [the aforementioned objects].
In the *Kālikāpurāṇa*:
"Having touched the remains of the offerings (*nirmālya*) of Rudra, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on."
Vyāsa states: Having touched the impure excretions of a vulture, a monkey, a cat, a donkey, a camel, as well as dogs and pigs, one should bathe along with one's clothes.
Āpastamba [Smṛti 9.10]:
"If the body should become defiled by the excrement of a crow or a crane, or if it should be smeared with impure substances..."
If it enters the ear or the mouth, purification is achieved by bathing and by cleansing with an application of clay.
“Viṣṭhitam” means caused by excrement. Śātātapa says:
“But he who touches an impure person defiles himself alone.”
Having touched that [object], another person [touches it], and he in turn by another; this is the procedure for all types of objects.
Parāśara [7.11–12]: When the sun has set, how is purification prescribed for one who touches a Caṇḍāla, an outcast, a woman, or a woman who has recently given birth?
[131] Having bathed with the permission of Brāhmaṇas and having seen Jātavedas, Suvarṇa, and likewise Somamārga, one becomes pure.
At night, there is no bathing in a pit or by a stream;
rather, bathing and sipping water (ācamana) are prescribed with water drawn up during the day.

“Ācāntam” means the sipping of water (*ācamana*). “Anugartam” means a reservoir of water. Here, the meaning is that both of these—“bathing” and “the sipping of water”—are stated as things to be performed. Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
“If, after the sun has set, one should touch anything untouchable during the night...”
Tell me with certainty: by what means can there be purification from worldly existence?
If water has been drawn before the sun has set, purification is achieved through that water in its entirety;
however, that which has been touched by a corpse is not purified by it.
Devala says: One should perform a bath at night with water collected during the day when there is a specific occasion,
having cast gold [into the water] and kindled a fire nearby.
Āpastamba: Upon touching an untouchable, after vomiting, upon the falling of a corpse, during menstruation, or after shaving,
one must perform an occasional bath (naimittika-snāna), excluding rites for the gods and ancestors.

“Bathing” (snāna) means that which is devoid of libations (tarpaṇa). “Devoid of rites for the gods and ancestors” (daivapitryavivarjita) means that which is devoid of the libations to the gods and ancestors that are ancillary to the bath.
Yama says: “When one who is ill reaches the occasion for bathing, he who is not ill should bathe ten times.”
Having bathed again and again, he should touch [the object] quickly; then that afflicted person becomes pure.
Now, the purification of substances.
Regarding this, Manu (5.111–122) states:
"For objects made of metal, for gems, and for all items made of clay,
purification has been declared by the wise to be by means of ashes, water, and earth."
An unblemished golden vessel is purified by water alone,
as are those made of lotus-fiber, stone, and silver, provided they are not otherwise treated.
Gold and silver emerged from the conjunction of water and fire;
therefore, their purification by means of their own source is more effective.
The purification of copper, iron, bell-metal, brass, tin,
and lead should be performed as appropriate with alkaline substances, acids, and water.
The purification for all liquid substances is declared to be straining;
for solid objects it is sprinkling, and for wooden items it is planing.
In the performance of a sacrifice, the cleansing of the sacrificial vessels is done with the hand,
whereas the purification of the *camasa* and *graha* cups is accomplished by washing.
The purification of the *caru* vessels and the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles is by means of hot water;
likewise for the wooden sword (*sphya*), the winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), the cart (*śakaṭa*), and the pestle and mortar (*musala-ulkhala*).
For large quantities of grain and clothing, purification is prescribed by sprinkling them with water;
however, for small quantities, purification by washing with water is ordained.
[134] The purification of skins is like that of clothes, and the same applies to articles made of split bamboo;
the purification of vegetables, roots, and fruits is held to be like that of grain.
Silk and woolen garments [are purified] with salts; blankets (*kutapa*) with *ariṣṭaka* fruits; fine cotton cloth (*aṃśupaṭṭa*) with bilva fruits; and linen with white mustard seeds.
For conch shells, horns, and objects made of bone or ivory,
purification should be performed by one who knows the rules using either cow’s urine or water, just as with linen cloth.
Grass, wood, and straw are purified by sprinkling;
a house by sweeping and smearing with cow-dung; and an earthen vessel by being fired again.

“Of metallic objects” refers to gold and the like; “of gems” refers to crystal and the like; “made of stone” means made of rock. Regarding the phrase “with ashes, water, or earth,” there is an option (*vikalpa*) between earth and ashes because they share the single purpose of removing stains and odors; however, water is to be used in conjunction with both. “Aquatic” refers to conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and so forth. “Unadorned” means free from markings and the like, since the presence of such markings implies the presence of impurity. “Purification” (*nirṇeka*) means cleansing. This rule concerns objects defiled by impure substances and the like. For copper, iron, bronze, and so forth, purification is performed with ashes, acid, water, or plain water as appropriate, provided no stain remains. “Of split-bamboo vessels” refers to those made from the slivers of bamboo and similar materials. “With saline earth” (*ūṣaiḥ*) means with alkaline soil. “*Kutapa*” is a specific type of woolen blanket.
In the Brahma Purāṇa: [Vessels] made of gold, silver, conch, stone, mother-of-pearl, and gems; and those made of bell-metal, iron, copper, brass, tin, and lead.
[135] Things that are not smeared with impurity are purified by water alone;
those defiled by the leavings of a Śūdra are to be cleansed three times with alkaline substances, acids, and water.
Items defiled by a woman in childbirth, a corpse, feces, urine, or a menstruating woman,
as well as whatever else one might endure, should be cast into the fire.
“Raityāni” means made of *rīti*, which is well known in the world as brass (*pittala*); such are they. [This refers to] Yama.
In every case, the vessel for the fruit is to be rubbed with cords of hair.
And one should sprinkle water upon the wooden sticks, as well as those made of bamboo and cow-dung.
All earthen objects are purified by burning again;
and for composite substances, purification is achieved with earth and water, as well as with clay.
The purification of all sacrificial vessels is prescribed by means of water;
the purification of grains is by sprinkling with water and by washing them with water.
The purification of hides is like that of clothes, and the same applies to articles made of split cane,
as well as for vegetables, roots, fruits, flowers, and seats.
The purification of wool and cotton is performed with water together with earth;
however, garments made of dukūla, paṭṭa, and kośeya are always purified by water alone.
“With a hair-rope” means with a rope made of cow-hair.
Likewise: “With *kutapa* wool for the *ariṣṭa* [robes], and with *śrīphala* nuts for the *aṃśu* and *patta* [robes].”
And with the hair of black antelope skins, and with earth and water from those hairs.
The purification of bones and teeth is by means of cow urine; that of linen garments is with white mustard seeds;
and that of dust-motes is by means of rolling [the garment] and with clay.
“*Pāṃsukaḥ*” refers to an altar (*vedī*) and the like made of dust. Yājñavalkya [1.76]:
Woolen and silken fabrics are purified by water mixed with soil and cow’s urine.
With *śrīphala* fruits he [prepared] a silk garment (*aṃśupaṭṭa*), and likewise, with *ariṣṭa* fruits, a woolen blanket (*kutapa*).
Śaṅkha says: For objects made of horn or ivory, purification is by means of a paste of white mustard seeds;
for vessels made of fruit, it is with cow-hair; and for bone, it should be as in the case of horn.
Likewise for resinous exudates, molasses, and salts;
and for safflower, saffron, wool, and cotton.
"Blessed Yama and Devala have stated that purification is declared to come from sprinkling [with water] for gold,
crystal, and silver, both in sacrifices and in ritual offerings."
And for the vessels of ascetics, purification with water is prescribed.
Likewise: "A cloth that was previously soiled to such an extent is purified by water and alkaline substances;
having dried it with rays of light, one may use it again, or [dispose of it] by means of the wind."
[137] For woolen cloth, fine silk, linen, cotton, and sheepskin,
purification occurs through a small amount of cleansing, as well as by sprinkling and other such means.
Those very [utensils] smeared with impurities should be washed with white mustard seeds,
with the pastes of grains, the pastes of leaves, juices, and the pastes of fruits.
Having dried pillows and other cushions, as well as flowers and red garments,
slightly in the sun, one should repeatedly wipe them with the hands.
Afterwards, having sprinkled them with water, one should declare, "They are pure";
then, those [objects] as well, even if excessively smeared, one should purify according to the rule.
The purification of metals is by burning, or by means of ashes or cow dung;
or for iron objects, it is by burning, or by digging, or even by water.

The purification of wooden objects is through planing; that of earthenware vessels is considered to be by means of fire. The purification of [objects] with clay and water is through cleansing with earth and water.
For all liquids, cooked foods, salt, molasses,
and everything that is impure, discarding them is prescribed.
In the absence of water, upon contact with another person, or even upon contact with the ground,
the abandonment or cremation of the water-pot (kuṇḍikā) is prescribed in times of distress.
For all remaining substances, purification is by means of water and fire;
indeed, both are prescribed by the Brahmins for the purpose of purifying everything.
Whatever substance a dog-cooker (śvapāka) might touch— whether it be an earthen vessel, a liquid, cooked food,
or a paste for eating— all of that one should avoid.
[138] That which is not liquid, when touched by remnants of food or impurities, is purified by water;
however, that which is liquid, even if it is abundant, one should purify by means of sprinkling and other such methods.
[The staff] of those made of deer-hair is [made] of lotus seeds.
Likewise [23.31–35].

Regarding large quantities of molasses and other products of sugarcane kept in the house, purification is by means of a strong fire. The same applies to all salts. For earthenware vessels, purification is by re-firing. For articles that have been purified like other objects, such as those used for the worship of deities, purification is by re-consecration. Regarding uncooked food that has been defiled, one should discard only that portion which was contaminated and perform the threshing and washing of the remainder. Thus says Hārīta.

[The purification] of golden and silver [vessels] is with water. For those damaged by oiliness or discoloration, cleansing is performed with the powder of barley, wheat, kalāya beans, māṣa beans, and cow dung, as well as washing with water. For copper vessels, it is with sour liquids and salt; for bell-metal (kāṃsya), with ashes; for black iron, with abrasion using emery; for tin, with striking and rubbing with sand; for gemstone vessels, with rubbing and cleansing on stone; for wooden vessels, with scraping; for earthenware, by re-firing; for wickerwork vessels, with cow urine, cow dung, and bilva fruits; for fruit-bowls, with a rope made of cow hair and water; for water-pots (kamaṇḍalu) and the vessels of ascetics, by wiping; for cotton and hemp fabrics, with alkaline substances and saline earth; for linen and silk garments, with putrajīvaka seeds and ariṣṭa; for woolen cloths, with putrajīvaka seeds and sour gruel; for silk (kauśeya), with bilva fruits and white mustard; for wool, with sour gruel, anthill earth, and mustard; and for skins, with oil, flour, and half-cooked grain (kulmāṣa) used as an ointment.
[139] “Kulmāṣas” refers to half-cooked beans. “Gurus” refers specifically to woolen blankets that have been soiled. In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
“Vessels smeared with milk products should be purified with hot water.”
"Gorasa-aktāni" means smeared with spoiled cow-products such as milk and the like;
thus state Śaṅkha and Likhita.

From this point forward is the rule for purification. The hand of an artisan is pure. Likewise, goods situated in a mine are pure when sprinkled with water. Edible items produced from mines are purified by being sprinkled with clarified butter (*ghṛta*). Oils are purified by straining. Solid substances that are oily are purified with earth and water. Liquid substances are purified by decanting. Dry substances are purified by removing the defect and then performing the proper refinement (*saṃskāra*). Defects that have been thoroughly washed away must be completely discarded. Clothes are purified with earth, ashes, cow-urine, alkaline water, or water. Grains are purified like clothes; the same applies to feathers, chowries, skins, grass, hair, cane, and bark.

“Edible substances produced from mines” refers to salt and the like. “Of fats” refers to ghee and so forth. “Of solid objects with earth and water”: for solid items such as beds and the like, purification is achieved by washing them with earth and water. “Of liquids” refers to molasses and the like. “Purification through the removal of defects” means that the very act of extracting the defect constitutes the purification. “Of defects that have been thoroughly saturated” refers to those that are completely permeated. Baudhāyana [1.8.28–43].

For metallic vessels, purification is performed by repeatedly scrubbing them with earth and ashes, or with one or another of these; for copper, silver, and gold, with acidic liquids; [for earthenware, by burning]; for wooden vessels, by planing; for bamboo, with cow-dung; for those made of fruit-wood, with a rope of cow-hair; for black antelope skins, with *bilva* husks; for woolen blankets (*kutapa*), with *ariṣṭa* fruits; for woolen cloth, by exposure to the sun; for linen, with a paste of white mustard; for cotton cloth, with earth; for leather, like cotton cloth; for stones and gems, like metallic vessels; for bone, like wood; for conch-shells, horn, mother-of-pearl, and ivory, like linen; or with milk; or by whatever means they become pleasing to the eye and the nose.
"Amatrāṇām" means of vessels. Paiṭhīnasi [says]:

Cups made of gold, silver, or copper that have the smell of remnants but no adhering stain are purified with water; those with adhering stains are purified with cow-dung, or with a mixture of cow-dung and clay-water. In this case, it makes no difference whether the vessel is broken or unbroken. Iron vessels are purified with sand and similar substances. Earthenware is purified by being fired again. Stone vessels are purified with water. Tin and lead vessels are purified with cow-dung and chaff. Bell-metal is purified with ashes. Wooden objects are purified by planing. Conch-shells, mother-of-pearl, and the like are purified with milk and water. Cloth is purified by washing. Stones and gems are purified in the same manner as cloth. Black antelope skins are purified with white mustard seeds. Skins of the Ruru deer and the goat are purified with *bilva* rice-grains. Blankets (*kutapa*) are purified with *ariṣṭa* fruits.

Uśanas: By smearing with wood-ash; by sprinkling roots, fruits, flowers, soil, grass, firewood, chaff, and grain; and by washing with water alone ropes, bamboo, sacrificial skins, cotton, linen, silk, fine Chinese silk, woven cloth, silk-garments, woolen cloth, and hair-cloth. Sumantu: [141]

The purification of gems, gold, silver, conch-shells, mother-of-pearl, stones, and corals is by scrubbing. The purification of garments, bamboo, ropes, and leather is by washing with water. The purification of ground, bones, and wood is by planing. The purification of earthenware and iron vessels is by heating over fire. The purification of lead, tin, copper, and iron is by scrubbing three times with water and ashes. The same applies to cow-hair ropes, flowers, fruits, leaves, and roots—except for those defiled by the remains of birds' food; in their case, there is no fault. The purification of cups (camasa) and other such items bitten by dogs, as well as of *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, *caru* pots, and other sacrificial implements, is by means of hot water. However, for metallic objects made of birch-bark, leather, hemp, bamboo, split cane, or bark, the purification is by washing with water.
Kāśyapa.

Now we shall explain the rules for the purification of vessels. Wooden vessels are purified by scraping. Those made of stone are purified by scrubbing with water. Earthenware is purified by burning again. Vessels made of bell-metal and copper are purified by wiping with acidic water. Bell-metal, tin, lead, copper, and iron are purified with ashes. Teeth, horn, conch, mother-of-pearl, and gems are purified with sand. Cloth, silver, and gold are purified with water. Grass, wood, *mūrja* grass, hemp, linen, bark-cloth, leather, bamboo, split-bamboo, leaves, and bark-cloths are purified in the same manner as cloth. Objects that are excessively defiled must be discarded.
In the *Vāyupurāṇa*: "Likewise, for [objects made of] ariṣṭa, bilva, and iṅguda wood, as well as for all items made of split bamboo, purification is prescribed to be the same as that for leather."
[142] The purification of all types of bark garments is held to be by means of ashes; likewise, the purification of bones, hides, wood, and horns is by scraping.
Or again, with a paste of gems, diamonds, corals, pearls, conch shells, and fruits, or with a paste of white mustard seeds or sesame seeds.
The purification of all woolen cloths and all sheepskins,
as well as that of cotton fabrics, is declared to be by means of ashes in every respect.
Hārīta says:

[The purification] of teeth is by means of water; of purchased goods, by threshing and winnowing; of rice, barley, and wheat, by rubbing, splitting, and grinding; of pulses (*śamīdhānya*), by husking, rubbing, and washing; of husked grains, by rubbing, washing, and circling fire around them (*paryagnikaraṇa*); of vegetables, roots, and fruits from commendable locations, by picking and washing; of sugarcane stalks, like pulses; of sacrificial materials and oblations, by cooking; of oils, by straining; of prepared salts, by re-cooking; and of grass and wood lying on the ground that have been touched by lotuses and the like, purification occurs upon the sight of an animal drinking from it.
“Of ivory” means made of ivory. “Pulses” refers to mung beans and the like. Āpastamba [1.17.9–13]:

One should eat from an earthen vessel that has not been specifically prescribed; if one has been prescribed, it must be fired with heat. Iron is purified by scrubbing; wood by scraping; and in the case of a sacrifice, according to the traditional injunctions.
[143] "It is traditionally taught (*āmnātam*) that it has been washed for another worldly purpose," according to the *Kapardibhāṣya*. Śātātapa states:
"In the case of bronze vessels smelled by a cow, or those containing the leavings of a Śūdra, [they must be purified] again."
And for objects defiled by a dog-cooker (outcaste), purification is achieved with ten applications of ashes.

Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "The purification of the *camasa* cups at a sacrifice consists in washing them with water; for the vessels of ascetics (*yatipātra*) at sacrificial rites, it is like that of the *camasas*. According to the traditional rule of the ascetics, there is scrubbing with water. Thus says the *Brahmapurāṇa*.
Numerous goods and non-goods are to be washed with water,
as are crops, rice, vegetables, roots, and fruits.
Baudhāyana [1.8.45–46]:

Regarding the sacrificial cups (*camasa*) in a sacrifice, because they are used for the proclamation [of the ritual], there is a Vedic revelation (*śruti*) stating, "They do not become defiled by Soma. However, for vegetables, roots, and fruits, there is purification through washing;
this follows from the rule of Śaṅkha and Likhita concerning purity.

The cleansing of leaves consists simply in washing them; those that have been used once are to be discarded. Likewise, for flowers, roots, and fruits, as well as for scattered (*viṣkira*) and shaken (*avadhūta*) grains, there is sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*); some say there is merely moistening (*abhyukṣaṇa*). For vehicles, beds, and seats, purification is the same as for solid objects. [144] "Scattered" refers to chickens and the like. Baudhāyana says:
A seat, a bed, a vehicle, boats, paths, and grass;
one's own bed, seat, clothing, wife, children, and water-pot.
These things are pure for oneself, but impure for others.
Hārīta states in continuation [of the rule regarding those] "defiled by false accusations, fallen, or afflicted by the odor or color of animals":

"Some maintain that vehicles, beds, and seats should be avoided; for there, due to the distinction of colors, the observation of contact between the pure and the impure, and the possibility of the transmission of disease through contact with the feet, separate purifications are better. When one's own [purification] is not possible, they prescribe wearing another clean garment. Upon touching [such things], one must indeed bathe with one's clothes on. For thus he says:
'One should use a seat, a bed, or a vehicle after having covered it [with a cloth].'"

Grass placed on unconsecrated ground is washed; that which has been defiled out of sight is sprinkled with water. The same applies to small fuel-sticks. When large pieces of wood are defiled, they are washed and dried; when many are defiled, they are merely sprinkled. Wooden vessels touched by food-leavings are scraped clean; those defiled by contact with leavings are planed down. Those defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and the like, must be discarded. This is except for specific instructions, such as those regarding the *agnihotra*, the *gharma* remnant, the *dadhigharma*, the *kuṇḍapāyināmayana*, the *utsargiṇām ayana*, the *dākṣāyaṇayajña*, the *aiḍādadha*, the *catuścakra*, and the *brahmaudana* offerings—in all these cases, there is washing with water and *darbha* grass. In all *soma* consumptions, the washing takes place at the *mārjālīya* shed using water alone. Those [vessels] defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and the like, are to be discarded. Metal vessels, having been rubbed clean as before, are washed. The materials for rubbing are cow dung, earth, and ashes. Those defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and the like, are to be remade or left to soak in cow's urine for seven nights, or likewise in a great river. Baskets woven of reeds, bamboo, *śara* grass, or *kuśa* grass are washed with cow dung and water. In the case of defilement of rice grains, they are washed and dried; in the case of husked rice (*taṇḍula*), they are discarded.
The *agnihotra*, *gharma*, *iḍādadha*, and so forth are specific names for ritual acts. "Mārjalīya" refers to the central area to the south of the *saumika* altar.
Paiṭhīnasi states: wood or grass that has been touched by a *caṇḍāla* or similar person becomes pure if one shows it to the sun.
Āpastamba [1.15.13–15]:

On a bed of grass spread by one who is ignorant, one should consider oneself pure provided that one does not touch others who are impure; likewise with grass and wood that have been buried. Or, having sprinkled it, one may use a garment.
Baudhāyana [1.13.14–15]: [The same].
One should not employ for divine purposes a garment that is worn out, mounted [on a frame], unwashed, or one that has been used by humans and not thoroughly purified. In the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"One should wash the garment every day for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors."
Everything defiled by feces, urine, or semen, however, must be purified with earth and water.
At the beginning of purification, that which is to be cleansed should be washed with cow’s urine, alkaline water, and plain water;
this applies to ropes, vessels made of bark, ladles, and skins.
[147] Having performed purification, there is then cleansing by rubbing with cow-hair;
for silken and woolen garments, much water mixed with silver should be applied.
Likewise, one should give [a garment] smeared with gold, as well as linen cloths and wet garments. Aṅgiras says:
"The purification of [woolen cloth] with a thousand fibers is by means of wind, fire, the sun, and the rays of the moon."
Woolen cloth that has been touched by semen or touched by a corpse is not defiled at all.
Those beds, seats, and vehicles that are bound with hair—
all these garments are said to be composite.
In the continuation of the phrase "of garments," Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"For all [garments], water, earth, brick, *iṅguda*, *bilva* leaves, rice, mustard paste, alkali, cow’s urine, cow dung, and so forth, are the substances for purification. Some say that for unwashed [garments], there is merely sprinkling.
As long as the odor and the stain caused by contact with impurity do not depart from an object smeared with it,
so long must earth and water be applied in all purifications of substances.
Viṣṇu [23.29]: "By sprinkling, [the purification of] things that are heaped together. Vasiṣṭha [3.48].
Purification for removing stains and odors consists of water and earth for that which is impure but not smeared.
Manu [5.128]: "The gods ordained three purifiers for Brāhmaṇas."
That which is unseen, that which is cleansed with water, and that which is praised by speech;
Vṛddhaśātātapa says:
"He who touches one who is impure is alone defiled;
another who touches him is not defiled. This rule applies to all objects."
If, among a collection of bowls, one should become impure, purification shall apply to that single one; it is not prescribed for the others.
Śaṅkha says:
That which arises from contact with impurity, and that by which something is defiled—its purification is declared to be that very thing; this is the general rule for effecting purity in such cases.
[149] 25 Now, the purification of those who are utterly corrupted.

In this regard, Viṣṇu [23.1–6] states: That which is defiled by bodily impurities, by *surā* liquors, or by intoxicants is "extremely defiled. All metal vessels that are extremely defiled are purified by casting them into fire. Those made of gems, stone, or shell are purified by burying them in the earth for seven nights. Those made of horn, ivory, or bone are purified by planing. One should discard those made of wood or clay. Regarding clothing that is extremely defiled, if the washed portion becomes free of stain, one should cut it away.
Here, the term "metal vessel" (*lohabhāṇḍa*) refers to a vessel made of a metallic substance.

Hārīta states: "Objects made entirely of metal that have been excessively defiled are purified by fire; objects made of earth, wood, or leather are to be discarded; according to some, only the defiled portion of garments should be cut away; however, the teachers maintain that for new garments, wearing them constitutes purification; therefore, the purification of all garments is achieved simply by washing. Śaṅkha and Likhita state: [the same].

For metallic objects defiled by semen, urine, or feces, purification consists of smelting, scraping, or wiping seven times with ashes. For cloth, it is by washing or cutting out the defiled portion. [150] "Smelting" means melting in fire. In this regard, since there are many methods of purification such as smelting and so forth, the application of these methods—whether immediate or delayed—is determined by the degree of contact between the substance to be purified and the defiling agent. Baudhāyana [1.8.43–44]:

For those items previously mentioned that have been touched by urine, feces, blood, semen, or a corpse, one should wipe them twenty-one times with any one of those same substances. Non-metallic objects in such a state should be discarded. For the aforementioned cow-dung and ashes, there should be washing with water and earth when they are thus excessively defiled. Woolen items are treated like clothing; bark garments bound with threads are treated like bark; and conch-shells are treated like [metal].
An object touched by intoxicants, urine, feces, phlegm, pus, tears, or blood cannot be purified at all; it is purified only by re-cooking.
Copper, gold, and silver that have been touched by these very [impurities],
as well as those that are extremely defiled, are prescribed to be discarded.
Likewise:
"Now, if a garment should be defiled by urine, feces, semen, or blood,
one should wash it again thereafter."
[151] If water that has been certainly defiled cannot be purified by [mere] water,
then it must be cut away or burnt, to the extent that it has become corrupted.
If it becomes impure by the falling of soil or charcoal, one should discard it.
Bṛhaspati [Āśaucakāṇḍa 75]: The purification of clothing, wickerwork, and leather is traditionally held to be washing;
however, if they are extremely defiled, one should discard that specific portion and cut it away for the sake of one's own purity.
Devala says:
"Defiled, avoided, wicked, and impure—these are the four kinds of impurity pertaining to those who bear sectarian marks (liṅgin); all of this shall be explained again."
Even a pure substance, when touched by something impure, is said to be defiled;
those things that are unfit to be eaten, chewed, or drunk shall now be described as things to be avoided in this context.
An outcast, one who has fallen from his caste, a Caṇḍāla, a village pig, a cock, and a dog—
these six should always be avoided according to the law.
A woman of the same caste, a woman who has recently given birth, one who is intoxicated, insane, or menstruating,
a relative of the deceased, and one who is impure— these eight should be avoided from their respective times.
Sweat, drops of tears, foam, discarded nails and hair,
and moist hide or blood— these the twice-born declare to be impure.
Human bone, a corpse, feces, semen, urine, menstrual blood,
a bloated carcass, and pus— these are declared to be "kaśmala" (filth).

It is taught that purification by sprinkling may occur according to the prescribed rule for things defiled; however, for those corrupted by foul substances, purification must always be achieved through cleansing and consecratory rites.
[152] 26 Now, the purification of the ground.
Regarding this, Manu [5.124] states: "By sweeping, by smearing with cow-dung, by sprinkling, by scraping,
and by the dwelling of cows, the ground is purified in five ways."
Yama says: By digging, by filling, by burning, by scraping, by scrubbing,
by treading with cows, and by the lapse of time— the earth is purified by these seven means.
Devala says:
Earth that has become impure is purified in five ways or four ways;
that which is defiled is cleansed in two or three ways, while that which is merely soiled is purified in one way.
Burning, digging the earth, smearing it, sowing seeds,
or sweeping— this is known as the fivefold purification.
Where a woman who has recently given birth, or a pregnant woman, or a human being dies; where Caṇḍālas reside, or where a corpse is deposited.
That which is defiled by feces and urine, and where corpses are seen—
in this way, the earth, abounding in such impurities, is perceived as unclean.
Where the earth is defiled by the footsteps of worms and insects,
it becomes corrupted by foul odors through the scattering and removal of drops of filth.
Covered with the impurities of nails, teeth, body hair, blood, semen, and menstrual discharge, or even by ashes, mud, and grass, it becomes defiled.

Baudhāyana [1.13.16–20]: For ground that has been struck, there is smearing with cow-dung; for ground that is full of holes, there is plowing; for ground that is damp, one should bring impure matter and cover it over. Ground is purified by four means: by treading upon it by cows, by digging, by burning, and by sprinkling; and by a fifth, by smearing with cow-dung; and by a sixth, by the lapse of time. Yājñavalkya [1.188]: [The same].
The purification of the ground is achieved by sweeping, burning, the passage of time, or the wandering of cows;
likewise, a house is purified by digging, scraping, smearing with cow-dung, sweeping, and plastering.
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: "The images of the gods, as well as their dwellings and temples—
whether external or internal— are commended when raised from the ground according to the scriptures."
Then the ground should be purified by means of water, cow-products, burning, scraping,
and sweeping, as well as by the five simple mantras.
Having removed [the soil] and washed it with water filtered through a strainer,
one should leave a distance of one hundred *daṇḍas* from a village and four times that from a city.
The ground is pure everywhere where no smearings are seen. Baudhāyana [1.9.11–12; 10.1]:
"The purification of the ground is achieved through sweeping, sprinkling, smearing, covering, and scraping, according to the specific defect and its location. Furthermore, they quote:"
"A drop of water the size of a cow's hide, when poured upon the ground, purifies it—whether the ground is covered with impurity or not—provided that no impurity is visible. Thus says Yama. [155]
One should always consider the ground in the dwelling of a Brahmin, likewise in a temple of the gods,
and also in a cow-pen to be pure.
Baudhāyana says: In the case of multiple marriages, wooden and stone structures are level with the ground, and bricks are used in a mixed manner.
Parāśara [7.34] says:
The mud and water on the road, boats, paths,
and grasses do not become defiled by touch, nor do structures built of baked bricks.
Having performed the cleansing three times sevenfold at step-wells, wells, tanks, gardens, and groves, purification is thus ordained.
Yājñavalkya and Viṣṇu [Yājñ 1.197; Vi. 23.41]:
Water from a road or mud that has been touched by outcastes, dogs, or crows is purified by wind alone, as are structures built of baked bricks.
Yājñavalkya [1.194]: "And roads are purified by the rays of the moon and sun and by the wind. Śātātapa: [156]

One should not take seven kinds of clay: from an anthill, from a place smeared [with excrement], from water, from a road, from a tree, from that which has been used for purification, and from what remains after purification.
There is no fault of being "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa) regarding water, nor regarding honey, nor clarified butter;
nor regarding fruits, nor hair, nor drinking vessels, nor women.
For the purpose of purification, one should not collect earth that contains pebbles, stones, or the like;
clay is traditionally said to be of three kinds: red, yellowish-white, and white.
[157] 27 Now, the purification by water.
In this regard, Manu [5.128] says:
"Water on the ground is pure where a cow would not feel thirst,
provided it is not contaminated by impurities and possesses its natural smell, color, and taste."
In the *Brahma Purāṇa*: Water situated on the ground is pure if it possesses fragrance, color, and taste, provided it is free from contact with hair, bones, corpses, feces, or urine.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
Water situated on the ground becomes pure, as does water resting upon a stone,
provided it is free from foul odors, colors, and tastes.
Water on the ground is meritorious where a cow would find no thirst; likewise, water situated on a stone is pure provided it is not contaminated by impurity.
[158] Yama said: A woman is not defiled by a paramour, nor fire by its act of burning,
nor water by urine and excrement, nor the twice-born by the performance of Vedic rites.
Cows do not become defiled while carrying nectar; women do not become defiled by having been enjoyed before;
and waters do not become defiled when situated upon the surface of the earth.
But a learned man should not be defiled by the acceptance of gifts.
Viṣṇu [23.44–46]: From a well from which a five-toed animal has died, or which is otherwise utterly defiled,
one should draw out all the water and purify the remainder with a cloth.
One should perform the kindling of the fire over a structure built with bricks baked in a pit;
thereafter, one should place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) upon that which has arisen from fresh water.
O Vasundharā, in the case of small, stagnant reservoirs, purification is said to be like that of a well; however, in large ones, there is no defilement.
Parāśara says:
Even from a minor offense committed against wells, embankments, or roads,
as well as against the water in those regions and in fields or paths where crops grow—
Manu declared that there is no fault in accepting food to be eaten or drunk;
however, water should be taken from all sources, such as ponds, wells, and tanks.
[159] But if one should later see impurity, one is purified by the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If water is defiled by being smeared with bone or skin, or contaminated by dogs, cats, or mice,
then purification should be performed at its bottom.
If water has fallen upon bones, skin, and so forth, or has been defiled by donkeys, monkeys, or pigs, one should draw out all such water; purification is achieved by thorough cleaning.
If a step-well, a well, or a pond should somehow become defiled,
one becomes pure by drawing out a hundred jars of water and purifying it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
When any kind of impurity sinks into wells,
one becomes pure by drawing out sixty jars of water and purifying them with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

Water possessing color, taste, and fragrance is pure; it is purified when drawn up from the earth by means of worn leather buckets, provided that a cow becomes free from thirst where it is found. Paiṭhīnasi states: [The same].

The waters contained within the earth are pure, endowed with fragrance, color, and taste, such that even a cow becomes free from thirst there. Even the "vast water" (*mahodaka*) is "perverted" (*viparyasta*).
It is called "perverted" because it has become possessed of tastes, fragrances, and so forth other than its natural taste. Devala says:
Water found on the earth that is free from odor, endowed with flavor, pure,
and not diminished by the drinking of cows, is considered most excellent.
Water that has been drawn out with pure vessels according to the prescribed rule is praised;
however, one should discard water that has been drawn out and has stood for even a single night.
There is no defilement for waters that are undisturbed and flowing freely;
however, when they are drawn out in small quantities, they may become defiled by impurities.
One should avoid from the sacred bathing sites (tīrtha) any stagnant ponds, rivers, wells, or lakes that are filled with filth and impurity.
Yājñavalkya [1.192]:
Water that is pure, which satisfies the cows, and which is naturally situated on the earth. Yama:
Water from a pond, from a forest, from a jar, from a well, from a trough, or water contained within a leather bag—
even if it comes from a Śūdra— is said to be undrinkable.
But one who has fallen into calamity may drink [water] from the ground.

[161] “Ghaṭaka” here refers to a water-jar or similar vessel prepared for the purpose of drawing up all the water from a well. “Kośa” is a leather bag. Even “without a Śūdra,” that [water] belonging to a Brāhmaṇa or other [caste] is not to be drunk. Hārīta says: “The waters situated on the ground are pure, except for those parts that have become impure. Water that has been drawn at night enters Varuṇa; therefore, one should not take [water] at night. One should take it while holding a fire above [the vessel], reciting ‘dhāmno dhāmnaḥ’.”

Baudhāyana [1.6.11–13]: Now, when the sun has set, the exponents of the Veda deliberate whether one should take water or not. "One should take it"—this is another view. As much water as he takes, for so long should he restrain his breaths. For Agni indeed takes up the water; thus says Uśanas.
Furthermore, Svāyambhuva Manu declared that wells, tanks, lakes, and rivers are not enclosed and are free from defects.
“Uncovered” means touched by *caṇḍālas* and others.
Bṛhaspati [Āśauca 77–78]:
That which is leftover, dirty, moist, or smeared with excrement;
All that is purified by water; how, then, can there be purification of water itself?
By the falling of the rays of the sun and moon, by contact with the wind, and by the urine and dung of cows, waters become pure; such is the established rule.
[163] 27–a Now, the purification of cooked food.
Regarding this, Manu says:
"A twice-born man should never eat foods that have turned sour;
having washed them, they become faultless when the time for the dharma of distress has arrived."
That which is mixed with lentils or black gram, as well as that which has stood overnight,
one should eat after washing it and sprinkling it with clarified butter.
Likewise, Yama says:
"If a fly, a hair, or the excrement of a mouse is seen fallen upon the food, or if it has been sneezed upon or shaken off [from the vessel],"
One should eat after touching [the food] with ashes or sprinkling it with water.
Food that has been sneezed upon, or seen by one with hair on the body, insects, moths, or worms;
by a menstruating woman, or by outcasts; or [polluted] by firebrands, ashes, water, or gold-water.
Manu has declared that food which is merely touched [by a dog] may be eaten.
[164] Likewise:
One should consume food that is praised by speech and avoid that which is defiled by speech;
for food and drink are pure when purified by speech—of this there is no doubt.
Flies, gadflies, mosquitoes, woodworms, and tiny ants—food touched by these is not defiled; these insects do not cause [the food] to be unfit for consumption.
Yājñavalkya [1.189]:
When food has been smelled by a cow, or likewise defiled by hair, flies, or insects,
earth, ashes, or water must be thrown into it for the sake of purification.
Baudhāyana [2.12.6]:

Having seen skin, hair, nails, insects, or mouse-dung, one should remove that portion of the food-ball (*piṇḍa*), sprinkle it with water, scatter ashes over it, sprinkle it again with water, and then consume it after it has been verbally consecrated as pure.
Regarding the term "unfit for consumption," Vasiṣṭha [2.14, 22–24] continues:

Cooked food that has been defiled by hair or insects [is generally unfit]. However, having removed the hair and insects, and having sprinkled it with water or scattered ashes over it, one may consume it if it is commended by word. Paiṭhīnasi says:
Food smelled by hair, insects, or a cow, or touched by gold or ashes, may be eaten after being sprinkled with water.

[165] Śātātapa says: Food that has been smelled by hair, insects, or a cow, or likewise defiled by a crow; or food touched by a eunuch, one accused of a crime, an outcast, a woman who has recently given birth, a menstruating woman, or an atheist—[is unfit to be eaten].
If food that has been seen [by such a person] should be present, its expiation is said to be this:
having sprinkled it with water and set aside a small portion, one should especially eat that.
One may touch food that has been smelled by a goat with ashes, or with water,
or even with gold and silver.
Ghee, milk-rice, milk, as well as sugarcane juice, molasses,
buttermilk contained in a Śūdra’s vessel, and honey— these do not become defiled.
“Pāyasa” refers to milk-rice and similar dishes; “takra,” however, is a derivative thereof. [Regarding] Uśanas:
[the purification of] foods by smelling them is [effected] by not smelling them; furthermore, [the purification of] fats, ghee, salt, honey, and molasses is by means of re-cooking.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"The purification of edible substances produced from mines is by sprinkling them with clarified butter; for oily substances, it is by re-cooking; for juices, it is like that of oily substances; for solid masses, it is with earth and water; for other materials, it is by straining; for dry items, it is by processing after the defect has been removed; and for defects that have soaked in, it is by discarding them. Baudhāyana [1.10.2–3] states:

For food that has been placed on the fire out of sight, one should illuminate it and sprinkle it with water; the same applies to foods purchased in the market. "Illuminating" means making it visible by means of a burning blade of grass or similar object.
Āpastamba [2.3.9]:
When food has been prepared out of sight, one should sprinkle it with water after placing it over the fire; this they call "the purification for the gods. Sumantu says:

Food defiled by hair, insects, spitting, or phlegm, or smelled by dogs, requires only sprinkling with water. Curd that has been left overnight must be cooked again. Food looked upon by a *caṇḍāla* is unfit to be eaten, except when purified by being touched with gold or water.
Devala says:
One should avoid food that has been looked upon by a Caṇḍāla, a dog, or even by monkeys or sheep, and food that has been dropped by cats and other such animals, as it is considered defiled.

[167] Hārīta states: When food is defiled by dogs, crows, vultures, hair, insects, ants, and the like; or when it has been touched by gold, silver, lapis lazuli, coral, or any such substance, or even by water that has been so touched—it becomes pure through sprinkling with mantras, carrying fire around it (paryagnikaraṇa), and being seen by the sun. In the case of a large quantity of food being defiled, one should remove a small portion from the defiled area, sprinkle the rest with water containing gold and silver, and it becomes pure. For liquids that are utterly defiled, however, there must be total abandonment. Baudhāyana [1.14.14–18] states:

The same applies to prepared sacrificial offerings (*siddhahavis*). If they have been defiled by dogs, crows, or similar creatures, one should remove the affected portion and sprinkle the remainder with water while reciting the section beginning with, “*Pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*. Regarding honey and water, purification occurs by transferring them from one vessel to another; the same applies to oil and clarified butter. If these are touched by what is ritually impure (*ucchiṣṭa*), one should throw them into water, retrieve them, and then use them.
The phrase “in this manner,” etc., extends this rule of transferring from one vessel to another. Beyond that, the specific prescriptions are not fixed. Viṣṇu [23.36–37]:

Food exceeding one *droṇa* in measure that has been prepared remains unspoiled even if it is contaminated. Having removed the contaminated portion from it, one should sprinkle water containing gold over it while consecrating it with the *gāyatrī*.
Parāśara states: "But food exceeding one *droṇa* in measure, even if defiled by parrots and other such creatures..."
For the sake of his purification, he should offer that which is not to be abandoned to the Brāhmaṇas.
Brahmins who know the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, and are deeply learned in the Dharmaśāstras,
having recited the Dharmaśāstra which has issued from the mouths of the sages, [should proceed].
The reciters of Dharma sing the teachings that follow from the mouth of the Sage;
that which is declared as Dharma by these is indeed the truth, and not otherwise.
For the sake of purifying more than a *droṇa* [of food], it is recited in the treatises on Dharma:
"One should not discard even a *droṇa* of food that has been licked by dogs or crows."
Having covered it and removed only that portion which has been struck by saliva,
one should sprinkle it with water infused with gold and heat it over a flame.
One should not avoid that food merely because it has been touched by the sacrificial fire;
having removed only that specific portion, the remainder deserves to be consecrated.
Solid objects are purified by sprinkling, and liquids by heating;
water, fire, and clarified butter become pure simply by touch.
One should declare that which has not been touched to be pure according to the Chāgaleya tradition.
That very same provision regarding the *droṇa* measure is for the purpose of showing the quantity of cooked food. Thus it is stated in the context of the aforementioned festivals:
"more than a *droṇa*" (Bṛhaspati, Saṃskāra 28):
"At a sacred ford (*tīrtha*), at a wedding, on journeys, in battle, or during a national calamity..."
In a city or during a village fire, there is no fault in touching what is touched or what is untouched.
Śātātapa says:
In a cow-pen, in a kitchen, in oil-presses, in the case of two mantras,
among women, children, and the sick, matters of purification are not to be scrutinized.
Hārīta says: "Food cooked in a closed vessel, food cooked in oil or ghee, milk-rice, curd, and parched grain— Manu declared these to be fit for those who do not eat the food of Śūdras."
[170] 28 Now, the refutations of impurity.
In this regard, Manu and Viṣṇu state:
"The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall;
a calf is pure while discharging milk; and a dog is pure when seizing game."
Manu, Vasiṣṭha, Śātātapa, and Baudhāyana state:
"A calf is pure when it causes milk to flow; a bird is pure when it causes fruit to fall;
women are pure during sexual intercourse; and a dog is pure when catching game."
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"The mouth of women, calves, birds,
and dogs is pure during sexual intercourse, while giving milk, when on a tree, and likewise during hunting."
Vasiṣṭha said:
"The deer killed tomorrow are already blessed; the fruit has been brought down by the deer themselves;
it has been traversed by children and frequented by women."
[171] Manu [5.131]: "Manu has declared that the meat of an animal killed by dogs is pure,
as is the meat of one killed by other carnivorous beasts, or by outcastes (caṇḍāla) and other such robbers."
Yama said: That which has been stepped over by children, that which has been walked upon by women,
and that which has been crawled over by mosquitoes and flies— this does not cause defilement.
The mouth of women, the back of cows, and the face of goats are faultless;
these are eternally pure, as is whatever is praised by speech.
Likewise: "One's own bed, seat, clothing, and even a child are always pure;
alms received by a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin) are always pure—this is the settled rule."
The wise do not find fault with a seat, a bed, a vehicle, the face of a woman, a goat-skin rug, a razor, nor likewise a sacrificial ladle during sacrifices.
A cow, a horse, droplets, a shadow, flies, locusts, parrots, a goat,
an elephant in battle, an umbrella, and the rays of the moon and sun.
[172] Earth, fire, the goat, wind, water, curd, clarified butter, and milk—
all these ten are eternally pure and fit for sacrifice.
Likewise: Fire is pure, the wind is pure, and those who move in the open air are purifying;
water is eternally pure, and a path is pure from being trodden.
Likewise:
Water that has reached the ground is pure; a woman devoted to her husband is pure;
a king intent on dharma is pure; and a contented Brāhmaṇa is pure.
That which is on the hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise displayed for sale,
almsfood mediated by a Brāhmaṇa, and all mines.

Sumantu says: Women, children, mosquitoes, flies, shadows, seats, beds, and droplets [of water] are always pure. There is no fault regarding jars of ghee or fruit-houses belonging to those whose food is otherwise unfit to be eaten.
The meaning is that even for those whose food is forbidden, jars of ghee and the like are not defiled.
[173] Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
Water from a river is pure; likewise, all mines are pure.
Merchandise displayed for sale is pure, and a horse facing toward victory is pure.
A cow is pure except for its mouth, and a cat is pure in its sequence [of actions];
Bṛhaspati [Ācāra 76] says:
"Women, children, and the elderly are never defiled."
Flies, droplets, women, earth, water, and fire—these do not defile.
A cat, a ladle, and a mongoose are always pure; Uśanas says that the hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise displayed for sale.
The sources [of merit] are the drinking of Soma and whatever is praised by speech.
Baudhāyana says:
A continuous stream that is not defiled, dust raised by the wind,
and all mines are pure, with the exception of a liquor mine.
Śātātapa says:
All particles of dust raised by the wind are pure,
with the exception of those from a donkey, a goat, a dog, a camel, or a dwelling place.
“Samūhanī” means a broom.
Baudhāyana [2.6.33–34] states:

“That one whose body is covered in the dust of the city, and whose eyes and face are filled with it—that person living in the city, even if self-controlled, will not attain perfection. This is not so.
Śātātapa says: There is no fault of being "leftover" (ucchiṣṭa) regarding water, nor regarding honey, nor clarified butter;
nor regarding fruits that are not cultivated, nor minerals, nor women.
Devala says:
Manu has declared that there are four kinds of purity for living beings in this world: *śuci*, *pūta*, *svayaṃ-śuddha*, and *pavitra*—these alone are called *medhya*.
Likewise: "Whether new or even stainless, an object is called 'pure' (śuci);
that which is clean, holy, and purified is designated as 'pure' (śuddha)."
For whatever substance, whether stationary or moving, has by itself alone attained a state of purity, that is traditionally known as "pure by itself."
That which, being itself unadulterated by other substances, purifies others,
and which is worthy of honor in offerings to the gods and ancestors— that is remembered as *pavitra* (the purifier).
Now, all grains, substances, and ornaments,
as well as varieties of food that are not to be rejected— these alone are pure.
The notion of purity arises regarding a substance that is free from impurities;
the notion of impurity arises regarding that very same substance when it is fit for ritual action.
Therefore, the twice-born call that which is pure, functional, and clean "śuci";
that which is stainless, prepared, and fit for ritual action is called "pūta."
The bladder, the cup, the vehicle, the mount, the implements,
the razor, and the seat— these are traditionally held to be pure by their very nature.
Children are inherently pure, as are women during their non-menstrual periods;
likewise, a Brahmin is never to be touched by women during their fertile seasons.
It is the settled rule that things acquired by inheritance are inherently pure;
likewise, it is recorded in the Smṛti that merchandise purchased from traders is considered pure.
The Blessed Manu declared that these three are pure: speech that is unblemished and praiseworthy, and that which is inherently pure and absolute.
A goat and a horse are pure in their mouths; cows are pure in their backs;
flowering trees are pure; and a Brāhmaṇa is pure in every respect.
Therefore, honey, gold, darbha grass, kutapa wool, sesame seeds, apāmārga, śirīṣa, lotus, āmalaka, and a gem;
Garlands, *sarvagā* grass, *dūrvā*, *sabhadrā*, and *priyaṅgu*;
unsifted sand, parched grain, turmeric, sandalwood, and barley.
Those produced from the palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, tulasī, and dhātrī trees—
these they declare to be pure for the purpose of sacrifice, whether for the offerings to the gods (havya) or the ancestors (kavya).
For embodied beings, there are things that nourish, remove impurities, and purify;
among these, fire and clay are especially purifying when used even once.
For the sake of purifying all impurities, for everyone, everywhere, and at all times,
[they are] fires kindled by those free from defilement, uncorrupted by wicked men.
He is capable of purifying all impurities;
it is taught that objects burnt by fire attain purity.
The purity of things touched merely by flames is certain;
however, there is no taking of fire that has been used by a *vṛṣala* except in times of distress.
The dog-cooker (śvapāka) and the vṛṣala are never worthy to consume [the food of] a Brāhmaṇa’s fire,
nor ever that of a Cāṇḍāla’s fire, an impure fire, or a funeral fire.
The learned do not prescribe the use of fire that has fallen out or fire from a funeral pyre;
however, cow dung situated in a pure place and removed from a cremation ground is auspicious.
Earth that is not from a village is pure when it is free from semen, feces, and urine. These are the exceptions to the rule regarding purification by heating.
Now, Manu and Viṣṇu [Manu 5.132; Vi. 23.51]:
The apertures above the navel are entirely pure;
those below are impure, as are the excretions that fall from the body.

Baudhāyana [1.10.18–19]: One engaged in ritual action should avoid touching anything below the navel. The Śruti states: "Indeed, that part of a person which is above the navel is pure, while that which is below is impure. Uśanas says:
The male person [was born] above the navel; the cow, fit for sacrifice, from the back; the goat from the mouth; and women from all parts. Their heart is impure. [178] Yama says:
A woman who has reached her menses is pure, as is wine in the mouths of women.
By contact, the wind, odors, tastes, and women do not become defiled.

The breath of women consists of the flavors of their mouths and their scent; from the mouth, a cow is impure, but it is traditionally held that a non-bovine animal is pure from the mouth. Likewise, a cow is pure behind its back, an elephant on its shoulder, and a horse is pure all over.
While the urine and feces of humans are indeed impure and mere filth,
it is an established principle that cow urine and cow dung are always pure.
Bṛhaspati [Saṃskāra 279; Āśauca 62–65]:
The feet of Brāhmaṇas are pure; the mouth of goats and horses is pure;
the backs of cows are pure; and all the limbs of women are pure.
The Moon enjoys her when the hair begins to grow; the Gandharva, upon the appearance of breasts;
the Sun, during the onset of menses; and the Fire-god enjoys the maiden at [the time of] menstruation.
Whether she has been enjoyed by force, or has fallen into the hands of thieves,
or has herself acted improperly, or has been neglected;
[179] Even a woman who has been utterly corrupted does not deserve to be abandoned;
for an expiation has been proclaimed for all, especially for women.
Women are an incomparable means of purification; they are never defiled. Month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their misdeeds.
Soma bestows purity upon them, Gandharva grants them auspicious speech, and Pāvaka provides their complete fitness for sacrifice; therefore, women are indeed worthy of sacrifice.
Yama said: A woman is not defiled by a paramour, nor fire by its act of burning,
nor water by urine and excrement, nor the twice-born by the performance of Vedic rites.
Cows do not become defiled while carrying nectar; nor are women defiled by having been enjoyed by another.
Just as waters situated upon the surface of the earth are not defiled,
so too a wise man is not defiled by the acceptance of gifts.

[180] Yājñavalkya [1.71–72]: Soma gave them purity, and the Gandharvas gave them beautiful speech; Pāvaka (Fire) gave them complete fitness for sacrifice; therefore, women are indeed sacrificially pure.
Purification is prescribed after her menstrual period in the case of infidelity;
however, abandonment is ordained in the event of pregnancy, or in cases such as the murder of the husband or other grave sins.

Yama says: A woman who has been enjoyed by force, or one who has fallen into the hands of thieves, or one who is deluded by the intoxication of passion, or one who is stupefied by liquor; [if she consents, she is not considered unchaste].
Whether she has herself fallen into misconduct or has been led astray by another, she shall be purified at the time of her menses; so too shall she who has become devoid of dharma.
A woman is purified by her menses; a river is purified by its current;
but she who observes the period of her menses is purified through union with a man.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:

"Prajāpati has declared that for women there is no vow, no ritual with mantras, and no religious duty. The traditional teaching of the sages is that a woman who has been taken by the hand (in marriage) does not incur fault even if she is approached by others when seeking offspring. For they are purified by their menses; Vaivasvata says that a pregnant woman is not purified [until after delivery], because purification by her menses is impossible during pregnancy. Hārīta says that engaging in sexual intercourse out of lust is an improper act. Gautama says that there is fault due to her being under a vow and because of the resulting conception. The teachers say that the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is the purifier for them, or else the Prājāpatya."

Hārīta says: One should avoid a woman who causes abortion, one who goes to a man of lower caste, one who goes to a pupil or a son, one who is addicted to drinking and vices, one who causes the depletion of wealth and grain, and likewise an unchaste woman. Some say that an unchaste woman is purified by her menses; others say that once she has abandoned sensual enjoyments, she is not to be shunned by others and incurs no fault.
Soma granted them purity, and the Gandharvas taught them speech.
And Agni [granted] the capacity to consume all things; therefore, women are most pure.
Thus say others.
Śaṅkha and Likhita state:
"Because they have failed in their single vow and because they have been corrupted by the senses of another, they become corrupters of the family."
Yama says: Even if a woman is of her own free will, her abandonment is ordained;
however, one must neither commit the murder of a woman nor cause the mutilation of her limbs.
[182] Vivasvat declared that for a woman who acts according to her own will and is unfaithful, there should be abandonment; one must avoid imprisonment, disfigurement, or execution for women.
Vasiṣṭha says: But four [wives] must be abandoned: she who has gone to a pupil, she who has gone to a teacher, she who especially kills her husband, and she who has approached a degraded man.
"Juṅgita" means censured.
Thus [is the work] by Bhaṭṭa Hṛdayadhara’s son, the Great Minister for Peace and War (Mahāsāndhivigrahika) of the illustrious Govindacandradeva, the Great King of Kings (Mahārājādhirāja).
The section on purification (*śuddhikāṇḍa*) in the *Kṛtyakalpataru* composed by the illustrious Lakṣmīdhara is completed.
